### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Burdick-Will, Bader, and Nguyen link computer-vision measures of the street environment within one straight-line mile of essentially every regular U.S. public school (78,416 schools in 14,147 districts, built from 164 million Google Street View images) to 2018–19 school-level chronic absenteeism, and show that within a district, schools whose surroundings contain more sidewalk and streetlight imagery have slightly lower chronic absenteeism after conditioning on school composition, tract socioeconomics, and image-based land-use controls. That association is the paper's one durable result and it is worth having: the sign is stable across all three specifications (sidewalks −.28, −.25, −.48 suburban; streetlights −.19, −.39, −.41 suburban; Table 3, p. 9), the standard errors are clustered at the district level with over 14,000 clusters, and the paper is the first national linkage of direct, image-derived walkability features to an education outcome. Readers should hold the magnitude in view, however, because the prose does not: one standard deviation of sidewalk imagery (27 percentage points of all images within a mile) or of streetlight imagery (10 points) moves the predicted rate by a quarter to two-fifths of a percentage point against a mean of 15.09 and a school-level SD of 11.87 (Table 2, p. 8), which is 2–4% of an SD, or roughly one to two chronically absent students in an average-size school. The design is a single cross-section with school-location rather than student-route exposure and no source of exogenous variation; the raw gradient actually runs the other way (high-absenteeism schools have more sidewalks and streetlights, Table 2), the streetlight coefficient doubles when the image-based controls are added (a change the text calls "somewhat"), and the paper never discusses whether commercial density is a confounder or part of the walkability bundle. The four sentences most likely to be quoted from it — "even small tweaks to the physical environment could lead to meaningful changes" (p. 2), "relatively cost-effective" (p. 10), the second hypothesis that direct measures beat road-network proxies (declared supported on p. 8), and the urban/suburban/rural story ("sidewalks only ... in suburban areas"; streetlights "twice as important in rural areas," p. 9) — all outrun the exhibits: no cost data are analyzed, crosswalks (a named "direct" measure) are null in every model, the proxy nulls arise in a joint model where sidewalks correlate .70–.71 with the proxies, and only two of ten metropolitan interactions reach p < .05, neither of them for streetlights. Add a cluster of text-versus-table slips (a misquoted SE, a dropped negative sign, a Discussion figure that understates the sidewalk coefficient, urbanicity shares in Table 2 that sum to 104–106%, an impossible population-density unit), an outcome attributed to the Office for Civil Rights for a year in which no CRDC wave was fielded, and the absence of any data, code, software, or supplementary-material statement for measures that no outside team can regenerate, and the right posture is: cite the paper for the existence and sign of a modest within-district association and for the feasibility of the measurement approach, read every number from Table 3 rather than the text, and do not lean on the causal, cost-effectiveness, proxy-versus-direct, or heterogeneity claims.

#### Key Strengths

- Scale and coverage: a near-census of U.S. regular public schools (78,416 in 14,147 districts, about 3% dropped for missing data; p. 3, Table 3 p. 9) joined to a national, systematically sampled image corpus (one point every 100 m of road, four headings, 164 million images; p. 4). This is the first national, school-level linkage of direct built-environment features to attendance, and it supplies a descriptive fact the field did not have.
- A sensible comparison design for an associational paper: district fixed effects absorb region, busing rules, state reporting definitions, and district attendance policy (pp. 6–7); standard errors are robust and district-clustered (p. 7); the control set is broad (grade span, charter/magnet, FRL, race, size, student–teacher ratio, tract advantage and disadvantage indices, car ownership, building age, density, and image-based land-use indicators), and test scores are deliberately excluded as post-treatment (p. 4).
- The core association is stable in sign across specifications and survives the addition of correlated image-based land-use controls (Model 1 to Model 2: sidewalks −.28 to −.25, streetlights −.19 to −.39; Table 3, p. 9), which is some reassurance that the walkability coefficients are not merely proxies for commercial density.
- The exhibits are internally coherent where they can be checked: every Model 1 coefficient and SE in the p. 8 prose matches Table 3; Figure 2's plotted points reproduce exactly from the Model 3 main effects plus interactions (suburban reference); Table 2's tercile Ns sum to 78,416 and its N-weighted tercile means reproduce the overall column.
- Candor about the outcome and the mechanism: the paper says chronic absenteeism is a "blunt" measure (pp. 4, 10), that it cannot separate bus-eligible from walk-zone students (p. 10), that perceived safety is subjective and unmeasured (p. 10), and it explains the image-timing gap (November 2019 imagery, 2018–19 outcome; p. 4) rather than hiding it.

#### Key Concerns

- Causal and policy language outruns an associational design. The estimand is a conditional within-district association; identification rests on selection on observables. Within-district siting of schools, residential sorting, tract-versus-attendance-zone mismatch (p. 4), traffic and crime exposure along arterials, and the raw reversed gradient (Table 2) are all live. Yet the paper writes of "effects" (p. 1; Figure 2 title), "small tweaks ... meaningful changes" (p. 2), "relatively cost-effective" (p. 10), and district busing-route advice (p. 10), and it compares its cross-sectional gradients to intervention effect sizes (Eklund et al., 2022; p. 10) as if they were like for like. No cost data appear anywhere.
- Hypothesis 2 ("direct measures ... will be better predictors ... than road network or intersection density," p. 3) is declared supported (p. 8) without being tested. The proxies' nulls come from a joint model in which sidewalks correlate .70 with image count and .71 with intersections (Table 1, p. 7); no proxies-only model, incremental R², or coefficient-equality test is reported; within-R² is .30 in every model; crosswalks, a named direct measure, are null throughout; and a significant intersections×urban interaction (−.38, SE .18; Table 3 continued, p. 9) that cuts against the claim is never mentioned in the text.
- The heterogeneity story is a point-estimate story. Of ten Model 3 interactions only sidewalk×urban (.40, SE .17) and intersections×urban (−.38, SE .18) reach p < .05; the streetlight interactions are .10 (.15) and −.22 (.22), so "twice as important in rural areas" (p. 9) and "highest in rural areas" (p. 10) rest on −.63 vs −.31 with heavily overlapping intervals (Figure 2, p. 6), and the rural sidewalk interval (roughly −.6 to +.6) contains the suburban estimate. Interactions with every other school and census variable were also run and are reported only as "no evidence of meaningful heterogeneity" (p. 8), with no table, so the metro result is one reported test from an unreported battery.
- The estimate depends on the control set, and the paper does not say so. Adding the image-based controls doubles the streetlight coefficient (−.19 to −.39) — described on p. 8 as not "a substantial change" — and those controls (signs, non-single-family homes) correlate .68 and .41 with streetlights (Table 1). Whether commercial density is a confounder, a mediator, or part of "walkability" is never discussed, and there is no sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding, no alternative radius, and no weighting by enrollment.
- Text–table and exhibit problems a reader must route around (all confirmed against the PDF): the Model 2 streetlight SE is ".11" in the text (p. 8) and ".12" in Table 3; the p. 7 text reports the non-single-family-home/greenery correlation as ".79" when Table 1 shows −.79; the Discussion's ".2 percentage point" sidewalk figure (p. 10) matches no Table 3 estimate (−.28, −.25, −.48) and contradicts p. 8's "a little more than a quarter"; Table 2's urban + suburban + rural shares sum to 103.85–105.72% although p. 4 defines them as mutually exclusive; Table 2's population density is labeled "1000s per square mile" with a mean of 403.39; the Middle-grades row is identical in the lowest and highest terciles; "average year built" (Tables 2–3) versus "median year" (p. 4); Table 3 never states that suburban is the omitted category or that the models include district fixed effects with clustered SEs.
- Reproducibility is weak for a 2026 article: no data-availability, code, software, or supplementary-material statement anywhere in the PDF (p. 11 back matter checked); the walkability and land-use measures depend on unshared classifier outputs (no architecture, seeds, labeled-set size, precision/recall, or image capture dates; pp. 4–6), so the key coefficients cannot be checked by anyone outside the author team; robustness claims (logged outcome, footnote 1; single-measure interactions, p. 7; the full heterogeneity battery, p. 8) carry no numbers; the sample-construction steps give no counts; and the outcome is attributed to the Office for Civil Rights for 2018–19 (p. 3), a year for which, to our knowledge, no Civil Rights Data Collection wave exists (the 10% definition and the year fit ED's EDFacts release, so the label rather than the year is the likely error, but the PDF cannot settle it).

#### What to Rely On

- Within U.S. school districts in 2018–19, regular public schools whose one-mile surroundings contain a higher share of images with sidewalks or streetlights had modestly lower chronic absenteeism rates after adjustment for school composition, tract socioeconomics, and image-based land-use indicators. Reference numbers: sidewalks −.25 to −.28 percentage points per SD (about 27 percentage points of imagery); streetlights −.19 to −.39 per SD (about 10 points); Table 3, Models 1–2, p. 9. Quote the range, not one column.
- The association is small in absolute terms: 2–4% of the cross-school SD (11.87) and 1.5–3% of the mean rate (15.09; Table 2, p. 8), or about one to two chronically absent students in a school of average enrollment (584).
- Crosswalk presence (measured as "any image within a mile"), image count, and intersection count show no independent association with chronic absenteeism once sidewalks and streetlights are in the model (Table 3, all columns) — a description of these specifications, not a verdict on crosswalks or on proxies (see below).
- Sidewalk and streetlight prevalence are substantially correlated with commercial and density indicators (sidewalks with signs .68, image count .70, intersections .71; streetlights with signs .68; Table 1, p. 7), and the raw gradient runs opposite to the adjusted one (highest-absenteeism tercile: sidewalks 44.45 vs 42.02, streetlights 15.56 vs 13.55; Table 2). The paper is a clean illustration of confounding by urban form in built-environment research.
- Feasibility: national, systematically sampled Street View imagery classified by CNNs can be aggregated to school buffers and linked to federal school data at scale (pp. 4–6). Cite the Nguyen-group papers (Q. C. Nguyen et al., 2019; Keralis et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2022) for the measures themselves and this paper for the school linkage.
- The reported CNN agreement rates (sidewalks 84.5%, streetlights 88%, crosswalks 97.2%, other indicators 82–95%; pp. 5–6) as the authors state them — with the caveat that they are raw percent agreement, not precision/recall.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Any causal reading ("effects," "small tweaks ... meaningful changes," p. 2) — the design is a single cross-section with school-location exposure, no exogenous variation, a reversed raw gradient, and coefficients that move with the control set.
- "Relatively cost-effective" and the crossing-guard comparison (p. 10) — no cost data are analyzed, crossing guards are unmeasured, and the paper's own crosswalk coefficient is null in every model.
- The unit of change: a "1 SD" shift in sidewalks is about 27 percentage points of all imagery within a one-mile radius (Table 2 SD 27.25; p. 10), on the order of tens of kilometers of road, not a tweak; and the associated change is a quarter of a percentage point of absenteeism.
- Hypothesis 2 and the Discussion's "direct measures beat proxies" claim (pp. 8, 10) — untested as stated (no proxies-only model, no fit or coefficient comparison), collinear regressors (.70–.71), crosswalks null, and an unmentioned significant intersections×urban interaction; cite for these specific image indicators only, not as evidence against walkability indices.
- "Sidewalks only matter in suburban areas" and "streetlights twice as important in rural areas" (p. 9; restated p. 10) — of the relevant interactions only sidewalk×urban is significant; the streetlight contrasts are non-significant point-estimate ratios; the rural sidewalk estimate is imprecise (CI ≈ −.6 to +.6), not a demonstrated zero; and the metro dimension is the one reported result from an unreported heterogeneity battery. Treat as exploratory, including the ambient-light and sidewalk-condition explanations offered for it.
- The streetlight magnitude: report −.19 to −.39 depending on whether signs and building-type indicators are controlled; the text's "does not lead to a substantial change" (p. 8) understates a doubling.
- The crosswalk null as evidence that crosswalks do not matter — 92% of schools have "any" crosswalk image within a mile (Table 2), and with about 3,000 images per buffer even a small false-positive rate saturates the indicator; the measure is nearly constant and uninformative.
- The prose numbers: Model 2 streetlight SE is .12 (Table 3), not .11 (p. 8); the non-single-family/greenery correlation is −.79 (Table 1), not ".79" (p. 7); the sidewalk association is −.25 to −.28 (Table 3), not ".2" (p. 10); census "physical environment" measures "do not vary dramatically" across terciles (p. 7–8) although population density nearly doubles (298 to 562; Table 2). Quote Table 3.
- Table 2's urbanicity rows and density units — shares sum to 104–106% against mutually exclusive definitions, and "1000s per square mile" is an impossible label; a replicator cannot tell which classification enters Model 3's interactions.
- The outcome source: "Office of Civil Rights ... 2018–19" (p. 3) with a 10% definition. Two sub-reviews and this synthesis independently note that the CRDC is biennial with no 2018–19 wave and that ED's 2018–19 school-level chronic-absence file is an EDFacts product; verify the file before replicating or benchmarking.
- Several supporting citations, per the literature sub-review's external checks (verify before repeating): Walk to School Day was started in 1997 by the Partnership for a Walkable America, not by the National Center for Safe Routes to School, which was created in 2006 (p. 3); Gottfried (2014) is a kindergarten study, not evidence on leaving school without graduating (p. 1); Gottfried (2017), cited three times, found bus riders less chronically absent than children arriving by any other mode including walking, which the paper does not mention; Yang et al. (2023) is cited for "more sidewalks, streetlights, and crosswalks" in lower-SES areas (p. 6) but appears to report only crosswalks; Carlson et al. (2017) and U.S. DOE (2019) document change in streets and lighting rather than stability (p. 4); the "around 28% in 2022–23" figure (p. 1) may belong to 2021–22.
- "A scale that was previously unimaginable" (p. 10) — national street-image social science (Gebru et al., 2017; Naik et al., 2017) and the authors' own 2019 national indicators predate this paper; the novelty is the school linkage, not the scale.
- Every unshown result — the logged-outcome check with 95 imputed zeros (footnote 1, p. 11), the single-measure interaction models (p. 7), and the null heterogeneity by grade span, FRL, race, car ownership, and other covariates (p. 8) — is author assertion with no numbers and no appendix.
- Generalizability beyond 2018–19: chronic absenteeism roughly doubled after the pandemic (p. 1), the identifying variation excludes single-school districts (their count is not reported), and rural estimates rest on comparatively few multi-school districts, which fits the wide rural intervals in Figure 2.
