### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper runs a national cross-sectional regression: about 78,000 schools, district fixed effects, district-clustered SEs, and a large set of school, tract, and image-based controls. That design is good enough to support its main descriptive claim. Within a district, schools with a higher share of Street View images showing sidewalks and streetlights inside a 1-mile radius have slightly lower chronic absenteeism, on the order of 0.2–0.4 percentage points per SD. The design does not identify causal effects, and several secondary claims go further than the evidence. These include the "effects" and policy language, the claim that direct measures beat network proxies (H2), and the urban/suburban/rural contrasts. The streetlight estimate doubles when image controls are added (Model 1 to Model 2), which shows that the headline magnitudes depend on which controls are included.

**Strengths:**

- The data are national and close to complete for the population: 78,416 regular public schools in 14,147 districts (Table 3, p. 9; Table 2, p. 8), with about 3% of schools that have valid locations dropped for missing data (p. 3). The walkability measures come from a published computer-vision pipeline covering 164 million images (p. 4), with per-feature accuracy reported (pp. 5–6) and pointers to validation work (Yue et al., 2022).
- District fixed effects remove confounding from region, district policy, busing rules, and district-level reporting practices (pp. 6–7). SEs are robust and clustered at the district level (p. 7), and 14,147 clusters is plenty for cluster-robust inference.
- The control set is broad and well reasoned. It includes school composition, tract advantage and disadvantage indices, car ownership, building age, density, and image-derived controls for commercial activity, housing type, greenness, fencing, and single-lane roads (pp. 3–4, 6; Table 3). Test scores are left out on purpose as a likely post-treatment variable (p. 4).
- The paper is open about the limits of the outcome (chronic absenteeism is "blunt," p. 4 and p. 10) and about the gap between image timing and outcome timing (p. 4).
- Table 3 matches the prose closely, and Figure 2 is arithmetically consistent with the Model 3 main effects plus interactions (checked below).

**Weaknesses:**

- **The design is associational, but the paper talks about effects.** Identification rests on selection on observables within districts. Several threats remain: residential sorting within districts, school siting (newer schools built on less walkable edges), tract variables that only approximate attendance zones (p. 4), unmeasured street safety and crime, and district-level placement of infrastructure. The paper uses "effects" (p. 2; Figure 2 title "marginal effect") and draws policy conclusions about building sidewalks and crossing guards (pp. 2, 10). Nothing in the paper tests the walking mechanism: there are no mode-share data, no placebo radius, and no dose-response by distance.
- **The estimates depend on the controls.** Adding the image controls moves streetlights from −.19 (SE .09) to −.39 (SE .12), about double (Table 3, Models 1–2, p. 9). The text calls this "does not lead to a substantial change" and says the coefficient "increases somewhat" (p. 8). The added controls are strongly correlated with streetlights: signs .68, non-single-family homes .41 (Table 1, p. 7). They could plausibly be part of the "walkable" bundle itself, or mediators, rather than confounders. The associations are only moderately significant: sidewalks t ≈ 2.3 in Model 2 (−.25/.11), streetlights t ≈ 2.1 in Model 1.
- **H2 is not a fair horse race.** Sidewalks correlate .70 with image count and .71 with intersections (Table 1, p. 7). Once sidewalks and streetlights are in the model, little independent variation is left in the network proxies. The paper never estimates the proxies without the direct measures and never formally tests whether the coefficients differ. The conclusion that proxies "do not predict" absenteeism (p. 8, p. 10) therefore does not follow from the specifications shown.
- **The heterogeneity claims are weaker than the prose suggests.** Of the ten Model 3 interactions, only sidewalk×urban (.40, SE .17) and intersections×urban (−.38, SE .18) reach p < .05 (Table 3 continued, p. 9). The claim that streetlights are "twice as important in rural areas as urban ones" (p. 9) and "highest in rural areas" (p. 10) rests on point estimates. Neither streetlight interaction is significant: urban .10 (.15), rural −.22 (.22). Heterogeneity was also searched across every school and census variable (pp. 7–8). Only metro location is reported as producing variation, and none of the null interaction results are shown. That is a multiple-comparisons and forking-paths concern.
- **Measurement problems with the crosswalk variable.** Crosswalks are measured as "any image within 1 mile shows a crosswalk," and 92.12% of schools have one (Table 2, p. 8). A school's radius contains about 3,000 images on average (Table 2). Even a small false-positive rate could turn this indicator on almost everywhere, and 97.2% accuracy (p. 5) says little about a rare class. The crosswalk null is therefore uninformative. It is not evidence that crosswalks don't matter.
- **Several descriptive-table anomalies (checkable).** The urban/suburban/rural shares add up to about 105% in every column of Table 2 (e.g., All: 45.27 + 44.82 + 14.99 = 105.08), even though p. 4 defines the categories as mutually exclusive. Population density is labeled "(1000s per square mile)" with a mean of 403.39 (Table 2), which is physically implausible and so almost certainly a units-label error. The student–teacher ratio has mean 20.97 and SD 31.64 (Table 2), which suggests uncleaned outliers. None of these directly overturns Table 3, but the Model 3 reference category depends on the urbanicity coding.
- **Several robustness claims are asserted but not shown:** the log-outcome specification with 95 imputed zeros (footnote 1, p. 11); near-normal residuals (footnote 1); "essentially identical" results when interacting one measure at a time (p. 7); and null heterogeneity by grade, car ownership, and other variables (p. 8). The 1-mile straight-line radius (p. 6) is justified but never varied.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the core result as a modest within-district association. Holding the controls fixed, a 1-SD higher share of sidewalk images (about 27 pp) goes with about 0.25–0.28 pp lower chronic absenteeism, and a 1-SD higher share of streetlight images (about 10 pp) goes with about 0.2–0.4 pp lower absenteeism (Table 3, Models 1–2, p. 9). The mean is 15.09% (Table 2, p. 8), so these are shifts of roughly 2% of the mean. They are not estimates of what building sidewalks or streetlights would do.
- For streetlights, report the range −.19 to −.39 rather than the Model 2 value alone. Which one you get depends on whether signs and building-type controls are included.
- Treat the urban/suburban/rural contrasts as exploratory. The only reliably estimated difference is that the sidewalk slope is flatter in urban than in suburban schools (sidewalk×urban .40, SE .17). The rural streetlight "twice as important" pattern is a point-estimate comparison with overlapping intervals (Figure 2, p. 6).
- Do not cite this paper as showing that network or intersection proxies are worse walkability measures than image-based ones (H2). The specifications cannot show that.
- Do not read the crosswalk null as evidence that crosswalks don't matter. The measure hardly varies (92% of schools have one) and is vulnerable to false positives.
- Before building on the data, check which absenteeism file was used. The paper says 2018–19 data "from the Office of Civil Rights" (p. 3). To my knowledge (external knowledge, not checkable in the paper), the Civil Rights Data Collection was fielded for 2017–18 and 2020–21 but not 2018–19, and 2018–19 school-level chronic absenteeism is usually released through EDFacts. The masking language on p. 3 also fits EDFacts. If the outcome is actually 2017–18, the gap between image timing and outcome timing is larger than stated.
- The N of 78,416 may overstate the identifying sample. The three-part R-squared reporting (within/between/overall; Table 3) suggests a routine that keeps single-school districts in the count. Those districts contribute nothing to within-district estimates. Rural estimates in particular probably rest on a small number of multi-school rural districts, which fits the wide rural intervals in Figure 2.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Design and identification.* The estimand is the conditional within-district association between school-surroundings infrastructure and the school's chronic absenteeism rate (Eq. 1, p. 7). District fixed effects are the right first step, since infrastructure standards, busing distances, and attendance-recording rules vary mainly across districts. Within a district, though, schools in walkable areas differ in many ways: they tend to be older, denser, more central, and closer to commercial corridors. Signs and non-single-family homes both predict higher absenteeism (.26* and .50***, Table 3 Model 2), so walkable places also carry correlates of high absenteeism. The authors control for these, and conditioning on them makes the walkability coefficients more negative. My interpretive reading is that this is the classic situation where the answer depends on whether commercial density is treated as a confounder or as part of the treatment. The paper does not discuss this choice, and it has no sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding (e.g., coefficient-stability bounds). A 0.2–0.4 pp association could easily be produced by modest unobserved sorting, so the causal and policy framing on pp. 2 and 10 goes beyond what the design can support.

*Exposure measurement.* The 1-mile straight-line buffer around the NCES coordinate (p. 6) is a sensible and transparent choice. It is not a measure of the routes students actually walk, and it matters differently by school type: high school and rural attendance zones extend far beyond 1 mile. In dense urban districts, buffers of nearby schools overlap heavily, which reduces within-district contrast. The image date (collected November 2019, p. 4) is a minor threat, because infrastructure changes slowly. Image capture years are not reported, however, and refresh rates likely differ between urban and rural roads. Classifier accuracy of 82–88% for sidewalks, streetlights, signs, and building type (pp. 5–6) is fine when averaged over thousands of images per school. The concern is error that differs by context, for example tree cover hiding sidewalks, and greenness is itself a covariate. The paper does not examine this.

*Estimation.* Linear FE with district-clustered robust SEs is appropriate. Unweighted school-level estimates describe the average school, not the average student. Footnote 1 (p. 11) cites near-normal residuals in defense of the untransformed outcome. That is not what matters under clustered inference, and the log check is not shown. Standardization makes coefficients comparable across walkability measures, but binary regressors (crosswalk, grade levels, charter, magnet, urbanicity) are presumably unstandardized. So the Figure 2 note that effects are "when the predictor changes by one standard deviation" (p. 6) is ambiguous for the crosswalk panel.

*What is load-bearing.* Solid: the negative within-district association for sidewalks (all three models) and for streetlights (all three models), conditional on the stated controls. Fragile: the size of the streetlight association; the suburban-only sidewalk pattern (the rural sidewalk interaction .48, SE .31, is not significant, so "only suburban" rests partly on a null); the rural streetlight amplification; H2. Unsupported by this design: causal and cost-effectiveness claims for sidewalk or crossing-guard investments.

*Checkable text-vs-table items:*

- p. 8 text, Model 1: sidewalks −.28 (s.e. .11), streetlights −.19 (.09), crosswalk .002 (.16), images .09 (.15), intersections −.05 (.12). Table 3 Model 1 (p. 9) matches exactly. **Consistent.**
- p. 8 text, Model 2: sidewalk "–.25 points (s.e. = .11)" matches Table 3 (−.25*, (.11)). The text gives streetlight "–.39 (s.e. = .11)", but Table 3 Model 2 shows "–.39*** (.12)". **Minor discrepancy in the SE.**
- p. 8 text says adding image controls "does not lead to a substantial change," and that streetlights "increases somewhat." Table 3 shows streetlights −.19 → −.39, a 105% increase in magnitude. **The prose understates the change.**
- p. 10 Discussion: "one standard deviation increase (around 10 percentage points)" in streetlights predicts "around 0.4 percentage point decrease." Table 2 (p. 8) gives streetlights SD 9.74, and Table 3 Model 2 gives −.39. **Consistent** (Model 1's −.19 goes unmentioned).
- p. 10 Discussion: "1 standard deviation (around 27 percentage points)" in sidewalks predicts a ".2 percentage point reduction." Table 2 gives sidewalk SD 27.25 (consistent). Table 3 gives −.25 (Model 2) and −.28 (Model 1), which p. 8 describes as "a little more than a quarter of a percentage point." **The ".2" understates the table and conflicts with the p. 8 wording.**
- Figure 2 (p. 6) vs Model 3 (p. 9), with suburban as the reference: sidewalks, suburban −.48, urban −.48+.40 = −.08, rural −.48+.48 = .00. Streetlights, suburban −.41, urban −.41+.10 = −.31, rural −.41−.22 = −.63. Crosswalks, suburban −.23, urban .15, rural .23. The Figure 2 point estimates match (read visually). **Consistent.** The p. 9 claim that streetlights are "twice as important in rural areas as urban ones" matches −.63/−.31 ≈ 2.0 arithmetically. However, the streetlight interactions are not significant (urban .10 (.15); rural −.22 (.22)), and the urban streetlight interval in Figure 2 ends just below zero (about −.02). "Strong relationship … everywhere" (p. 9) therefore overstates the urban case.
- p. 9 claim that sidewalks "only have a strong relationship … in suburban areas": the urban difference is significant (.40*, SE .17). The rural difference (.48, SE .31) is not, and the rural sidewalk interval in Figure 2 is very wide (about −.57 to .56). **Partly supported.**
- p. 7 text: the "strongest correlation is between the presence of non-single-family homes and greenery (.79)." Table 1 (p. 7) shows −.79. **The sign is dropped in the text.** The claim that non-single-family homes, greenery, and fencing are "not highly correlated" with the walkability measures sits against Table 1 values of .44/.41 (non-single-family homes), −.31/−.43 (greenery), and signs at .68 with both sidewalks and streetlights. These are moderate to high. Correlations are pooled across all schools, not within districts, so they do not speak to collinearity in the FE models.
- Sample size: p. 3 "more than 78,000" matches Table 2 N = 78,416. Tercile Ns 25,877 + 25,878 + 26,661 = 78,416 (Table 2). Table 3 reports 78,416 schools and 14,147 districts in all models. **Consistent.** Singleton districts are not reported.
- Table 2, "more than five times" the absenteeism in the top vs bottom third (p. 7): 27.47/5.33 = 5.15. **Consistent.**
- Table 2 urbanicity shares add up to more than 100% in every column (103.85, 105.72, 105.64, 105.08), even though p. 4 defines the categories as mutually exclusive. **Inconsistent; unexplained.**
- Table 2: population density "(1000s per square mile)" mean 403.39. **Implausible units label.** "Middle" grades has identical values (37.26, SD 48.35) in the lowest and highest thirds, which may be a transcription error. The table says "average year built," while p. 4 says "median year." **Minor label mismatch.**
- Image timing (p. 4): images collected November 2019 for a 2018–19 outcome. The authors' justification is plausible but uses no data, since image capture dates are not reported. The OCR attribution for 2018–19 absenteeism (p. 3) should be verified (see Guidance).
- Eq. (2) (p. 7) says all five walkability measures are interacted at once. Model 3 has 5 × 2 = 10 interaction terms (Table 3 continued). **Consistent.** The claims that single-measure interactions are "essentially identical" (p. 7), that heterogeneity by other school and census variables is null (p. 8), and that the log-outcome results match (footnote 1, p. 11) are **not shown and not verifiable** from the article (no appendix available to this review).
- Significance stars vs coef/SE (Table 3): most agree after allowing for rounding. Two are borderline: Model 1 sidewalks −.28/.11 (t ≈ 2.55, marked **), and Model 2 streetlights −.39/.12 (t ≈ 3.25, marked ***). Both are explainable by SE rounding. **No clear error.**

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper sets out a short, coherent argument that ties three literatures together: structural barriers to attendance, the effect of the built environment on walking (including children's active travel to school), and virtual or computer-vision neighborhood audits. Its reference list is clean: every in-text citation I checked appears in it, and I found no uncited entries. For a short *ER* Feature Article, its central framing is fair. The problems are in the details. Several supporting citations are stretched, anachronistic, or wrong about data sources and years. The best causal evidence that safer commutes raise attendance, Chicago's Safe Passage studies, is missing. The paper also does not engage evidence that walking as a travel mode is associated with *more* absence than riding the bus, and one of those studies (Gottfried, 2017) is in its own reference list. Its claim that direct measures beat "proxy" walkability measures (Hypothesis 2) is also made without the walkability-index literature that would test it most directly.

**Strengths:**

- **Clear interdisciplinary synthesis.** Pages 1–3 connect education research on absenteeism (Balfanz & Byrnes, 2012; Gottfried, 2014, 2017, 2019; Childs & Lofton, 2021) with urban-planning and public-health work on walkability (Fonseca et al., 2022; H. Wang & Yang, 2019; Y. Wang et al., 2016; Ellis et al., 2016) and on children's active school travel (Christiansen et al., 2014; Rothman et al., 2021; Molina-García et al., 2020). The "structural barriers" framing (p. 2) cites a solid set of recent sources (Gottfried & Gee, 2017; Kearney et al., 2023; Lenhoff et al., 2021; Singer et al., 2021; Ballentine et al., 2025).
- **Good coverage of the transportation-and-attendance core.** The paper cites Gottfried (2017), Stein & Grigg (2019), Edwards (2023), Cordes & Schwartz (2019), Burdick-Will & Stein (2024), Burdick-Will et al. (2019), and Lenhoff et al. (2021, 2023) (pp. 1–3). That is most of the canonical U.S. work.
- **Fair lineage for the measurement approach.** The paper traces image-based measurement from in-person systematic social observation (Sampson & Raudenbush, 1999) to virtual audits (Odgers et al., 2012; Bader et al., 2017; McCoy et al., 2022) and then to deep learning (Starzyńska-Grześ et al., 2023; Yue et al., 2022; Keralis et al., 2020; Q. C. Nguyen et al., 2019, 2022; T. T. Nguyen et al., 2021) (pp. 3, 5–6). It openly says the image data come from the authors' earlier work.
- **Clean bibliography.** I found an exact match in both directions between in-text citations and the reference list (see Checkable items). The problems are with what the sources are said to show, not with missing entries.
- **Measured novelty claims.** The paper never says "first." Its only explicit novelty language is "novel machine-learning estimates" (p. 1) and "a scale that was previously unimaginable" (p. 10). The second overreaches (see below), but the article does not claim priority over studies it has not searched for.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The source and definition of the outcome data are probably misstated (checkable).** The paper says school-level chronic absenteeism "come[s] from the Office of Civil Rights during the 2018–19 school year" (p. 3, "Chronic Absenteeism"). It defines the measure as missing more than 10% of school days (p. 4). Two problems follow. First, when the Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC) did collect chronic absenteeism, it defined it as 15 or more days absent, not 10%. Second, the Department of Education stopped collecting the item through the CRDC starting with 2017–18 and moved it to EDFacts, beginning with 2016–17 data (verified through the ED/ECS CRDC documentation found by search). From my own knowledge, the CRDC is biennial and had no 2018–19 wave. The data are most likely EDFacts / ED Data Express files, which use a state-implemented 10%-type definition. If so, the definition in the paper is roughly right but the attribution is wrong. Readers who reuse or replicate these data should check the source.
- **The headline absenteeism statistics mix sources, definitions, and possibly years (checkable).** The 13% pre-pandemic figure (p. 1) comes from a secondary Florida literature review (Humm Patnode et al., 2018). As far as I know, it matches the 2013–14 CRDC figure, which uses the 15-day definition. The "around 28% in the 2022–23 school year" figure (p. 1, citing US Department of Education, 2025) does not match the AEI and FutureEd trackers I found by search. They put the ~28% peak in 2021–22 and about 25% in 2022–23. I could not open the cited ed.gov page (HTTP 403), so treat this as "verify before repeating," not as a confirmed error. The paper's own sample mean for 2018–19 is 15.09% (p. 8, Table 2), which is a better pre-pandemic benchmark than 13%.
- **Walking vs. riding the bus: conflicting evidence goes unengaged (checkable).** Gottfried (2017), cited on pp. 1, 2, and 10, found that kindergartners who rode the school bus were less likely to be chronically absent than children who got to school any other way, *including walking* (verified by search). Lenhoff et al. (2023), also cited, found that Detroit students who walked or biked daily had *better* attendance than those driven by a parent (verified from the working paper). So the evidence on whether walking to school protects attendance is mixed and depends on the comparison group. The paper cites both studies for other points (p. 2; p. 3, where Lenhoff et al. is used for walking as a backup when other transportation fails). It never tells readers that its mechanism, "students can walk when other options fail," sits alongside evidence that walkers attend *less* than bus riders. This is the main gap in how the paper engages conflicting evidence.
- **The strongest causal evidence on commute safety and attendance is missing (judgment).** Chicago's Safe Passage program has been studied with quasi-experimental designs. McMillen, Sarmiento-Barbieri & Singh (2019, *Journal of Urban Economics*) and Gonzalez & Komisarow (2020, Annenberg EdWorkingPaper, "Can Community Crime Monitoring Reduce Student Absenteeism?") both report attendance gains when route safety improves (confirmed by search; the ~1.7-point attendance estimate I saw reported for McMillen et al. should be checked in the original). This is the closest causal evidence for the paper's first proposed mechanism (p. 3), yet the paper supports that mechanism only with its own associational Chicago study (Burdick-Will et al., 2019).
- **The "direct measures vs. proxies" claim lacks its natural comparison (judgment).** Hypothesis 2 (p. 3) and the Discussion ("these general proxies for walkability do not predict social behavior in this context as well as direct measures," p. 10) set sidewalks and streetlights against image counts and intersection counts. They never cite the literature on composite walkability indices: Frank and colleagues' walkability index; Ewing & Cervero's (2010, *JAPA*) meta-analysis of the "D" variables, which finds intersection density among the stronger built-environment predictors of walking; or the EPA's national Smart Location Database / National Walkability Index. A standard, national, off-the-shelf walkability proxy already exists, and the paper does not benchmark against it. The within-district null for intersection count (p. 8, Table 3: –.05, s.e. .12 in Model 1) is therefore weak evidence against "proxies" in general. Readers should cite this paper for *these particular* image-derived indicators, not as evidence that direct measures dominate walkability indices.
- **Several supporting citations are stretched (checkable; details below).** Examples: Gottfried (2014), a kindergarten study, is cited for dropping out without graduating (p. 1). Carlson et al. (2017) and U.S. Department of Energy (2019) are cited for the claim that the physical environment is stable (p. 4), although they document policy-driven change in streets and lighting. Chalkley et al. (2018) is cited for barriers from "physical infrastructure nearby" (p. 3), but it is about on-site space for a school running program. Lawrence et al. (1997) and Y. Liu et al. (2016, 2021) are cited for CNNs being state of the art (p. 4); these are face-recognition, climate, and food-science papers. The paper also credits the National Center for Safe Routes to School with starting Walk to School Day in 1997 (p. 3), an anachronism.
- **Thin engagement with the Safe Routes to School evidence base (judgment).** The NCSRTS is cited only for descriptive mode shares (p. 2) and an awareness day (p. 3). The federal SRTS infrastructure program and its evaluations are absent: effects on walking and biking (e.g., McDonald et al., 2014, *JAPA*) and on child pedestrian injuries (e.g., DiMaggio & Li, 2013, *Pediatrics*). That program is the most direct policy test of the paper's policy claim that sidewalk investment is "relatively malleable" and cheap (p. 10).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **What to cite this paper for.** This appears to be the first national, within-district association between computer-vision-derived sidewalk and streetlight prevalence around schools and school-level chronic absenteeism. My targeted searches found no earlier study of that exact pairing, though I cannot rule out gray literature. Do not cite it as the origin of the image data. The national GSV indicators come from the Nguyen group (Q. C. Nguyen et al., 2019; Keralis et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2022). Do not cite it as causal evidence either. The paper sometimes uses "effects" language (p. 1; p. 10), but the design is a cross-sectional district-fixed-effects regression.
- **Verify before repeating:** (a) the outcome-data source and definition (p. 3–4; see above); (b) the 13% and 28% national figures and their years (p. 1); (c) the one-third active-transport figure for students within one mile (p. 2). The third comes from NCSRTS trend data, which to my understanding are drawn mainly from parent surveys at schools taking part in SRTS programs, not a nationally representative sample. The National Household Travel Survey (cited on p. 2 but not used for numbers) is the representative source. The 15% walking and 2% biking figures (p. 2) are consistent with my recollection of the 2016 NCSRTS report.
- **Companion readings on commute safety and attendance:** McMillen, Sarmiento-Barbieri & Singh (2019) and Gonzalez & Komisarow (2020) on Safe Passage; Cordes, Rick & Schwartz (2022, *EEPA*) on long bus rides and absences; Blagg, Rosenboom & Chingos (2018, Urban Institute), "The Extra Mile," on travel time and outcomes in DC. Read Gottfried (2017) in full for the bus-versus-walking comparison.
- **Companion readings on walkability and children's school travel (U.S.-centered):** McDonald (2007, 2008) on the decline in walking to school and the role of distance; McMillan (2005, 2007) on how parents decide whether children walk, which is central to the paper's argument on pp. 2–3; Zhu & Lee (2008, *AJPM*) on walkability and safety around elementary schools and their economic and ethnic disparities, a direct antecedent audit study; Ewing & Cervero (2010) and Frank et al. on walkability indices; and McDonald (2010) and the EPA's (2011) school siting guidelines on why schools within a district differ in walkability. The paper's own active-travel citations are mostly European and Canadian (Christiansen, Denmark; Molina-García, Spain; Chillón, UK; Müller, Germany; Rothman, Canada). That matters because U.S. distances, busing policy, and car ownership are different.
- **Companion readings on computer vision and street imagery:** Gebru et al. (2017, *PNAS*), which used about 50 million GSV images across 200 U.S. cities; Naik, Kominers, Raskar, Glaeser & Hidalgo (2017, *PNAS*) on detecting urban change; and review articles such as Biljecki & Ito (2021) and Rzotkiewicz et al. (2018). These show that national-scale street-image measurement was established well before this paper, which tempers the "previously unimaginable" framing (p. 10).
- **Economics context that changes the reading:** Schools near busy roads have more traffic pollution, and pollution increases absences (Currie, Hanushek, Kahn, Neidell & Rivkin, 2009, *REStat*; Heissel, Persico & Simon, 2022, *JHR*). Sidewalks and streetlights are concentrated along arterials (compare the sidewalk–sign and sidewalk–intersection correlations of .68 and .71 in Table 1, p. 7), so this literature points to a confounder the paper does not discuss. It would, if anything, bias *against* the paper's negative coefficients, which readers may find reassuring. The literature on school start times and morning darkness is relevant to the streetlight results (p. 9, Figure 2; streetlights matter most in rural areas) and is also not engaged.
- **Measurement-accuracy context:** The classifier agreement rates reported (sidewalks 84.5%, streetlights 88%, crosswalks 97.2%; p. 5; other indicators p. 6) are raw percent agreement. For a rare class such as crosswalks, high agreement can come mostly from the base rate. The paper refers readers to Yue et al. (2022) and does not report class-balanced metrics. Check that source before treating the crosswalk null (p. 8) as substantive.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Overall structure.* The review runs in three steps. First, attendance has structural causes. Second, walking depends on infrastructure. Third, infrastructure can now be measured at scale. The logic is sound and fits *ER*'s cross-disciplinary readership. Qualitative work is represented only lightly: Chalkley et al. (2018) and Marchant et al. (2020) are qualitative or mixed-methods studies of school running programs, and two local news stories (Dahms, 2025; Papst, 2022, p. 3) stand in for parents' experiences. In my judgment, qualitative and survey studies of how parents decide whether children walk (McMillan's framework; the parent-perception studies in the SRTS literature) would have supported the p. 2–3 mechanism better than news reports.

*The three mechanisms (p. 3), checked against the literature.* (1) "Dangerous commutes are known to discourage student attendance" cites Burdick-Will et al. (2019). That study is about exposure to *violent crime* along routes, while the paper's walkability argument is mostly about *traffic* danger: sidewalks, crosswalks, streetlights. Traffic danger has its own literature on child pedestrian injury and the built environment, and none of it is cited. The two dangers point to different interventions (crossing guards and sidewalks versus Safe Passage–style monitoring), and streetlights plausibly work through both. (2) "Walking as backup when motorized transport fails" cites a 2023 AEFP conference paper (Lenhoff et al.). I obtained that paper. Its main finding is that daily walkers and bikers in Detroit had higher attendance than students driven by a parent, net of covariates. It supports the direction of the paper's argument but is not direct evidence of a backup mechanism. (3) The physical-activity → health → attendance chain relies on an intervention meta-analysis (Jones et al., 2019), a meta-analysis on physical activity and achievement (Fedewa & Ahn, 2011), and two UK running-program studies. It is the most speculative link and is presented with appropriate hedging ("likely," p. 3).

*Novelty and placement.* The paper's real contribution is to link an existing national image-derived dataset to a national school outcome, with district fixed effects. That contribution is modest but real. The rhetoric around it overstates in two places. First, "at a scale that was previously unimaginable" (p. 10) ignores national street-image work that is nearly a decade old (Gebru et al., 2017), including the authors' own 2019 national indicators. Second, the implied contrast with "labor-intensive" audits (p. 3) undersells McCoy et al. (2022, *AERA Open*), which audited school surroundings with Google Street View in an education journal and is the closest education-field antecedent. The paper cites it only as an example of a small-scale method. In the other direction, the paper probably *undersells* how rarely the education literature has measured the physical surroundings of schools at all, and that gap is what makes the contribution useful.

*Effect-size framing (p. 10).* The paper compares its within-district standardized associations (about 0.2–0.4 percentage points per SD; p. 8, Table 3; p. 10) with the small effects of individual attendance interventions (Eklund et al., 2022). That treats an observational association as comparable to experimental intervention effects, and no literature on sidewalk or streetlight costs is cited for the claim that installing sidewalks costs "minimal" amounts (p. 10). These are interpretive leaps rather than citation errors, but readers should not repeat the cost-effectiveness framing as though it rested on evidence in the paper.

*Chronic-absenteeism measurement literature.* The paper acknowledges that chronic absenteeism is a "blunt measure" (pp. 4, 10) and cites Humm Patnode et al. (2018) and Childs & Lofton (2021). It does not engage the work showing that states define and count absences differently, or the literature on measuring absence more finely: part-day absence (Whitney & Liu, 2017, *AERA Open*), the value of absence counts versus thresholds (Gershenson, Jacknowitz & Brannegan, 2017, *EFP*), and tardiness, which the first author has studied (Burdick-Will & Stein, 2024, cited on p. 1 only as a transportation study). District fixed effects absorb most state-level definitional differences, as the paper notes (p. 7), so this omission affects context more than validity.

**Checkable items** (citation and reference-list checks performed; page = where the in-text citation appears)

1. Humm Patnode et al., 2018 (p. 1, 13% figure): **in reference list**. It is a secondary source, and the figure appears to be the 2013–14 CRDC rate under the 15-day definition. *Verdict: present; the figure is not directly comparable to the 10% definition used later.*
2. US Department of Education, 2025 (p. 1, "around 28% in the 2022–23 school year"): **in reference list**. The AEI and FutureEd trackers put ~28% in 2021–22 and ~25% in 2022–23. I could not open the ed.gov page. *Verdict: possible year error; verify.*
3. Gottfried, 2014 (p. 1, disengagement and "leave school without graduating"): **in reference list**. Search confirms it is a nationally representative *kindergarten* sample with achievement and engagement outcomes. *Verdict: the engagement claim is supported; the dropout or non-graduation claim is not.*
4. Liu et al., 2021 (p. 1): **in reference list**, but two different "Liu 2021" entries exist (J. Liu, Lee & Gershenson; Y. Liu, Pu & Sun), and only the second gets an initial in text (p. 4). *Verdict: minor ambiguity; the p. 1 citation means J. Liu et al. (J Public Econ), whose characterization is fair.*
5. Gottfried, 2017 (pp. 1, 2, 10): **in reference list**. Its finding favors bus riders over *all* other modes, walking included (verified). *Verdict: accurately cited for what the paper uses it for, but the paper leaves out the finding that cuts against its thesis.*
6. Edwards, 2023 (pp. 1, 2): **in reference list**, listed as *EFP* 19(1). Volume 19 is the 2024 volume, so the year likely reflects online-first publication. *Verdict: present; minor year inconsistency.*
7. Cordes & Schwartz, 2019 (p. 1): **in reference list** (Urban Institute report on pupil transportation and access to school quality). *Verdict: present; fair as an example of transportation research that is not about walking.*
8. Stein & Grigg, 2019 (p. 2): **in reference list**. *Verdict: fair (public-transit use and absenteeism in Baltimore).*
9. Balfanz & Byrnes, 2012 (pp. 2, 6): **in reference list**, cited as the *Education Digest* condensation rather than the original Everyone Graduates Center report. *Verdict: the three-category taxonomy is fairly paraphrased.*
10. Weathers et al., 2021 (p. 2, policing and truancy leading to criminal-justice involvement): **in reference list**. *Verdict: present; I could not verify that this specific claim appears in the systematic review.*
11. National Center for Safe Routes to School, 2016 (p. 2; 15% walk, 2% bike, about one-third active travel within one mile): **in reference list**. *Verdict: present; the figures match my recollection of the report, but the underlying parent-survey data are, to my understanding, not nationally representative.*
12. Walk & Roll to School Day "started" by the NCSRTS "in 1997" (p. 3, no citation): **not a reference-list item**. Search confirms U.S. Walk to School Day was started in 1997 by the Partnership for a Walkable America, and the NCSRTS was created in May 2006 and later became the national coordinator. *Verdict: factual error (anachronism).*
13. Lenhoff et al., 2023 (p. 3): **in reference list** (AEFP conference paper; author order differs slightly from the paper's own suggested citation). *Verdict: present; supports walking being associated with better attendance than car travel, not specifically a "backup" mechanism.*
14. Chalkley et al., 2018 (p. 3, "schools without adequate physical infrastructure nearby"): **in reference list**. It is a qualitative evaluation of the Marathon Kids program in English primary schools. The barriers reported were lost curriculum time, *on-site* space constraints, and weather (verified by search). *Verdict: stretched characterization.*
15. Marchant et al., 2020 (p. 3, "before-school activities or running clubs"): **in reference list**. The Daily Mile happens during the school day. *Verdict: loose fit.*
16. McCoy et al., 2022; Odgers et al., 2012; Sampson & Raudenbush, 1999 (p. 3): **all in reference list**. *Verdict: fair collectively. Note that Sampson & Raudenbush used video recorded in person, not an online tool, which the sentence's "either... or" structure allows.*
17. Bader et al., 2017; Starzyńska-Grześ et al., 2023 (p. 3): **in reference list**. *Verdict: fair.*
18. Carlson et al., 2017; U.S. Department of Energy, 2019 (p. 4, physical environment "unlikely" to change "substantially and systematically"): **both in reference list**. Carlson documents the spread of Complete Streets *policies*. The DOE report forecasts solid-state (LED) lighting adoption, which to my knowledge includes rapid streetlight conversion around 2017–2019. *Verdict: these sources document change more than stability; weak support for the claim.*
19. Lawrence et al., 1997; Y. Liu et al., 2016, 2021 (p. 4, CNNs "state-of-the-art" for object detection and scene labeling): **in reference list**. The Lawrence entry is garbled, repeating the article title where the journal should be (it is *IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks*, 8(1)). The Liu papers apply CNNs to climate data and food science. *Verdict: present but off-target; standard computer-vision references are absent.*
20. Yue et al., 2022; Keralis et al., 2020; Q. C. Nguyen et al., 2019, 2022; T. T. Nguyen et al., 2021 (pp. 5–6): **all in reference list**. *Verdict: fair; these are the authors' own data-lineage citations.*
21. Chillón et al., 2015 (p. 6, one-mile threshold): **in reference list**. It is a longitudinal UK (Norfolk) study. *Verdict: present; generalizing it to U.S. mode choice is a stretch, and U.S. distance studies (McDonald, 2008) would fit better. The companion claim that districts rarely bus within one mile has no citation.*
22. Yang et al., 2023 (p. 6, lower-SES students live where there are "more sidewalks, streetlights, and crosswalks"): **in reference list**. On PMC, the abstract reports more *crosswalks* in predominantly minoritized neighborhoods, attributed to older, pedestrian-oriented development. Sidewalks were not among the five final indicators analyzed, and streetlights were not reported in the abstract. *Verdict: partially supported (crosswalks); the sidewalk and streetlight parts go beyond the source as I could verify it.*
23. Owens & Candipan, 2019 (p. 4, school tract correlated with students' residences): **in reference list**. *Verdict: present; I did not verify the specific claim.*
24. Molina-García et al., 2020 (pp. 2, 9): **in reference list**. *Verdict: fair; used appropriately to interpret urban and rural differences.*
25. Eklund et al., 2022; Childs & Lofton, 2021; Jimenez, 2024 (p. 10): **all in reference list**. *Verdict: present; the Eklund comparison is interpretive (see above).*
26. **Reverse check (reference list → text):** I went through all of roughly 60 reference entries (pp. 11–13), and each one is cited somewhere in the text. *Verdict: no orphan references.*
27. **Data-source attribution (p. 3–4):** "Office of Civil Rights ... 2018–19" chronic absenteeism with a 10% definition. The CRDC used a 15-day definition and moved chronic absenteeism to EDFacts beginning with 2016–17 data (verified via the ED/ECS documents found by search). From my own knowledge, there was no 2018–19 CRDC wave. *Verdict: likely misattributed; verify.*

**Missing or under-engaged work** (my judgment; not an exhaustive search, and I may miss niche work)

- *Commute safety and attendance, causal:* McMillen, Sarmiento-Barbieri & Singh (2019); Gonzalez & Komisarow (2020), both on Chicago Safe Passage. Also the literature on walking school buses (e.g., Mendoza et al., 2011, *Pediatrics*).
- *School transportation and absence:* Cordes, Rick & Schwartz (2022, *EEPA*); Blagg, Rosenboom & Chingos (2018); Gottfried's later rural bus-ridership work (a 2021 *Early Childhood Research Quarterly* article on bus ridership and absenteeism in rural communities turned up in search). I also recommend a fuller account of Gottfried (2017)'s comparison of walking and bus riding.
- *Safe Routes to School evaluations:* McDonald et al. (2014, *JAPA*) on walking and biking outcomes; DiMaggio & Li (2013, *Pediatrics*) on pedestrian injuries. The SRTS program itself (federal funding since 2005) is not mentioned.
- *U.S. children's travel and parental decisions:* McDonald (2007, 2008); McMillan (2005, 2007); Ewing, Schroeer & Greene (2004) on school location and travel; McDonald (2010) and EPA (2011) on school siting; Zhu & Lee (2008) on walkability disparities around schools.
- *Walkability indices (the "proxy" side of Hypothesis 2):* Frank et al.'s walkability index; Ewing & Cervero (2010); the EPA National Walkability Index.
- *Street-image and computer-vision social science:* Gebru et al. (2017); Naik et al. (2017); Glaeser, Kominers, Luca & Naik (2018); reviews by Biljecki & Ito (2021) and Rzotkiewicz et al. (2018). Also Q. C. Nguyen et al.'s earlier 2018 "Neighbourhood looking glass" paper, if I recall its date correctly.
- *Environmental confounders from economics:* Currie et al. (2009) and Heissel, Persico & Simon (2022) on traffic pollution near schools and absences.
- *Absence measurement:* Gershenson, Jacknowitz & Brannegan (2017); Whitney & Liu (2017). My search also surfaced a 2026 EdWorkingPaper, "The Chronic(les) of Absenteeism Measurement." I have not read it and do not characterize it.
- *Neighborhood effects on absence in education:* Gottfried (2014, *Urban Education*), "Can Neighbor Attributes Predict School Absences?" I also noticed a recent PMC article on nearby arrests, violent crime, and absenteeism but did not read it.

*Limits of this review.* Online appendices were not available, and I have not assessed anything that may be there. I verified web-accessible items (the CRDC definition and collection change, Gottfried 2017 and 2014, the Lenhoff et al. 2023 findings, the Walk to School Day history, Chalkley 2018, the Yang 2023 abstract, the Safe Passage studies, and the absenteeism trend figures from secondary trackers). I could not open the ed.gov page cited for the 28% figure. Items marked "to my knowledge" or "as I recall" come from my own background knowledge and should be checked.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is a short, plainly written paper with a conventional structure: framing, two stated hypotheses, data, analysis, results, discussion. A reader can find the main result quickly (Table 3, p. 9) and most of the numbers quoted from it are reproduced correctly. The exposition is still less reliable than its tidy surface suggests. I found several checkable text-versus-exhibit slips: a misquoted standard error, a correlation reported without its negative sign, a Table 2 summary that one row of the table contradicts, a Discussion restatement that understates the sidewalk coefficient, and urbanicity shares that add up to more than 100%. The heterogeneity prose (p. 9) and the "support for both hypotheses" sentence (p. 8) claim more than the reported estimates and intervals support. None of these reverses the headline association, but readers should check any number against the tables before quoting it.

**Strengths:**

- *(Interpretive)* The paper is compact and easy to follow. The two hypotheses are stated explicitly (p. 3) and addressed by name in the Results (p. 8, "This model provides support for both hypotheses"). The design (within-district comparison via district fixed effects, p. 6–7) is explained in plain language before the equations.
- *(Checkable)* Every Model 1 coefficient and SE quoted in the p. 8 prose matches Table 3 (sidewalks –.28/.11, streetlights –.19/.09, crosswalk .002/.16, images .09/.15, intersections –.05/.12). The p. 8 prose also translates standardized coefficients into plain terms ("a little more than a quarter of a percentage point"; "approximately one-fifth").
- *(Checkable)* Table 2's "All" column is internally consistent. N-weighted averages of the three tercile columns reproduce the All-column means (e.g., chronic absenteeism 15.10 vs. 15.09 reported; sidewalks 42.33; streetlights 14.46; population density 403.39). The tercile Ns (25,877 + 25,878 + 26,661) sum to the reported 78,416, which also matches Table 3's "Number of schools."
- *(Checkable)* Figure 2's plotted points match the linear combinations of Table 3 Model 3 main effects and interactions (details below). The figure really does display Model 3, and its error bars are consistent with 95% intervals built from the Table 3 SEs.
- *(Interpretive)* The measurement section (pp. 4–6) is candid about the timing mismatch between the November 2019 imagery and the 2018–19 outcome. It explains why crosswalks are coded as "any" rather than as a percentage, which a reader needs in order to interpret that coefficient.

**Weaknesses:**

- *(Checkable)* **Text–table mismatches.** (a) p. 8 gives the Model 2 streetlight SE as ".11", but Table 3 shows "(.12)". (b) p. 7 calls the non-single-family home–greenery correlation ".79", but Table 1 shows "–.79". The sign flips the substantive meaning. (c) p. 7–8 says the census physical-environment measures "do not vary dramatically across groups", yet Table 2 population density rises from 298.11 (lowest third) to 561.55 (highest third), nearly doubling. (d) p. 10 says a 1-SD sidewalk increase "predicts a .2 percentage point reduction". No sidewalk coefficient in Table 3 rounds to .2 (–.28, –.25, –.48), and the p. 8 prose itself described the Model 1 value as "a little more than a quarter."
- *(Checkable)* **Table 2 internal problems.** The Urban + Suburban + Rural shares add up to 103.85% (lowest third), 105.72% (middle), 105.64% (highest), and 105.08% (All). But p. 4 defines the three categories as mutually exclusive (central city / in-metro non-central city / outside metro). The population-density unit label, "(1000s per square mile)", would make the mean 403,390 persons per square mile, which is not plausible. "Middle (serves grades 6-8)" is identical in the lowest and highest thirds, 37.26 (48.35). The All column (37.60) is consistent with this within rounding, so it may be genuine, but it looks like a possible duplication.
- *(Interpretive, anchored in checkable values)* **The heterogeneity prose overstates.** p. 9 says sidewalks "only have a strong relationship ... in suburban areas" and streetlights are "twice as important in rural areas as urban ones." The point estimates support the ratios (streetlights: rural –.63 vs. urban –.31). But of the two relevant interactions for streetlights, neither is significant (Streetlights*urban .10 (.15); Streetlights*rural –.22 (.22)). The rural sidewalk interval in Figure 2 runs from about –0.58 to +0.56, which easily contains the suburban estimate (–.48). The prose never uses the words "significant" or "interval" for these contrasts.
- *(Interpretive)* **Hypothesis 2 is declared supported although part of it fails.** H2 (p. 3) names "sidewalks, streetlights, and crosswalks" as better predictors than road network or intersection density. Crosswalks are null in every model (Table 3), and "better predictor" is judged only by which coefficients cross p < .05. No comparison is formally tested. "Support for both hypotheses" (p. 8) is stronger than "partial support for H2."
- *(Checkable)* **Unshown and undiscussed results.** p. 7 ("Results are essentially identical if we only interact one ... at a time") and p. 8 ("We do not find evidence of meaningful heterogeneity"; the car-ownership interaction) describe estimates that appear in no exhibit. No online appendix was available to me, so I could not verify them. Conversely, Table 3 Model 3 reports a significant Intersections*urban interaction (–.38*, SE .18) that the prose never mentions. It is relevant to the p. 10 claim that intersection density does "not predict chronic absenteeism."
- *(Checkable)* **Exhibit self-containment.** Table 3 does not state the omitted metro category, so readers must infer that suburban is the reference. That means Model 3's "Sidewalk –.48***" is the suburban slope, not an average. The table also does not note district fixed effects or district-clustered SEs, which appear only in the text (p. 7). Figure 2 has no y-axis label and does not state its interval level. Its caption title ("Predicted marginal effect") differs from the in-figure title ("Average Marginal Effect by Metropolitan Location"). The p. 9 text says Figure 2 shows "sidewalks and streetlights," but the figure has a third, crosswalks panel.
- *(Checkable)* **Production errors.** "Author's calculations" appears as the source line on Tables 1–3 and Figure 2 of a three-author paper. The sentence ending "(Chalkley et al., 2018)" on p. 3 has no period. p. 7 has "car ownerships." In equation (2) on p. 7, β1 is reused for both the main effect and the interaction term. The same variable is labeled "Not-single-family" in the Table 1 header, Table 2, and p. 8 prose, but "Non-single-family" in the Table 1 row, Table 3, and p. 5. It is "Street Lights" in Figure 2 but "Streetlights" everywhere else. p. 10 has a stray comma: "socioeconomic status, and urban development."

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Must read:** the hypotheses (p. 3); the measure definitions on p. 6 (percent of images within a 1-mile straight-line radius; crosswalk coded as "any"); the Analysis section (pp. 6–7); Table 3 (p. 9); Figure 2 (p. 6); and the Results prose on p. 8. These carry the whole argument.
- **Can skim:** the literature framing on pp. 2–3 and the CNN training paragraph on pp. 4–5, which is mostly deferred to Yue et al. (2022). Also skim Table 1 (p. 7) once you note that sidewalks correlate .67–.71 with streetlights, images, intersections, and signs.
- **Before quoting a number:** use Table 3, not the prose. For the Model 2 streetlight SE, use .12 (not .11). For the sidewalk effect, use –.25 to –.28 pp per SD (Models 1–2), not ".2." The Table 1 NSF–greenery correlation is negative (–.79).
- **Reading Model 3:** Model 3's "Sidewalk" and "Streetlights" rows are **suburban** slopes. Urban and rural slopes are the main effect plus the interaction (e.g., rural streetlights = –.41 + (–.22) = –.63; rural sidewalks = –.48 + .48 = 0.00). Differences across metro types are mostly not statistically significant. The only significant sidewalk contrast is urban vs. suburban (.40*).
- **Keep the magnitudes in view** *(my calculation from Tables 2–3)*. The largest average association, streetlights in Model 2 (–.39 pp per SD), is about 2.6% of the mean school chronic absenteeism rate (15.09%) and about 0.03 SD of its cross-school distribution (SD 11.87). The abstract gives no magnitudes.
- **Watch the raw gradient.** In Table 2, high-absenteeism schools have *more* sidewalks (44.45 vs. 42.02) and streetlights (15.56 vs. 13.55) than low-absenteeism schools. The negative regression coefficients appear only after within-district adjustment. The prose alludes to "a complicated pattern of confounding" (p. 8) but never says outright that the sign reverses.
- **Interpret Table 2's urbanicity rows cautiously** (the shares add up to more than 100%). Treat its population-density units as unreliable.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Organization and navigability (interpretive).* The paper runs about ten pages of text and follows a standard IMRaD order, with a hypotheses subsection that helps orient the reader. There are two navigation problems. First, Figure 2 is typeset on p. 6, in the middle of the measures section and before the Analysis section, but it is first cited on p. 9. A reader meets a heterogeneity figure before being told any model exists. Second, Table 3 spans two columns of p. 9. Its "(continued)" block, which holds the interaction terms, R², and Ns, sits to the right, beside the text that interprets it. That is readable in print, but plain-text or screen-reader extraction puts it before the main coefficients. The load-bearing material sits in three places: Table 3, Figure 2, and the p. 8 prose. The Discussion (p. 10) mostly restates rather than adds.

*Abstract fidelity (interpretive, with checkable anchors).* The abstract states the question, data, design ("compare schools in the same district"), and direction of the finding accurately, and it uses appropriately associational phrasing ("tend to have lower"). What it leaves out matters. It gives no magnitudes; the effects are a fraction of a percentage point per SD (Table 3). It does not mention the null results for crosswalks and for road/intersection density, although H2 turns on them. It does not mention the urbanicity heterogeneity, which the introduction (p. 1) and Discussion (p. 10) both highlight. Its final sentence, "physical infrastructure can be an important structural barrier to attendance," leans on "important" more than associations of roughly 0.2–0.4 pp can carry. Elsewhere the body slips into causal vocabulary: "The magnitude of these effects" (p. 1); "even small tweaks to the physical environment could lead to meaningful changes" (p. 2); "places where it is easier for students to walk to school" (p. 10, although walking is never measured). The design is cross-sectional and observational, so readers should treat "effect" language as shorthand for conditional associations.

*Fidelity of argument (interpretive).* Models 1–2 support the core claim that within districts, sidewalk and streetlight prevalence is negatively associated with chronic absenteeism, net of the listed controls. Three stretches go beyond the exhibits. (1) The p. 9 heterogeneity paragraph turns point-estimate contrasts into categorical statements ("only," "twice as important," "everywhere"). The urban streetlight interval in Figure 2 barely excludes zero (upper bound ≈ –0.03), which is weak grounds for "strong relationship ... everywhere." (2) The p. 8 hypothesis verdict ignores the crosswalk null. (3) The p. 10 methodological claim, that image and intersection density "do not predict chronic absenteeism," is stated as a clean result. But these proxies correlate .70–.71 with sidewalks (Table 1), so their nulls in a joint model are partly a question of shared variance. Model 3 also shows a significant urban intersection interaction. Also, p. 8 introduces the heterogeneity tests as a check for "nonlinearities." Interactions test effect modification, not nonlinearity, and a reader could come away thinking functional form was examined.

*Tables and figures (mixed).* Table 3 is the paper's central exhibit and is clean apart from the missing reference category, FE indicator, and SE-clustering note. The two-sided layout works on the page. Table 2 is useful but carries the problems listed above: shares over 100%, an implausible density unit, and "average year built" in the table vs. "median year" on p. 4. The neighborhood advantage index has SD 0.77 in Table 2 although p. 4 calls it a "standardized sum." That is plausibly standardized at the tract rather than school level, but it is not stated (ambiguous). Table 1 is a lower-triangle correlation matrix with no N or note, and its column and row labels disagree ("Not-single-family" / "Non-single-family"). Figure 1 is illustrative only. Figure 2 is honest in scale: all three panels share a –1 to 1 axis, and the axis is not truncated to exaggerate contrasts. But it lacks a y-axis label and interval definition. Its note says effects are "when the predictor changes by one standard deviation," but the crosswalk predictor is binary. The Table 3 note says only "continuous variables have been standardized," so the crosswalk panel's scaling is ambiguous.

*Density and length (interpretive).* The paper is short enough that a time-constrained reader can read pp. 3 and 6–10 in full. The main cost of the brevity is that robustness claims (single-interaction versions, other heterogeneity dimensions, the logged outcome in footnote 1) are asserted rather than shown. No appendix was available for this review, so I cannot say whether they are documented elsewhere.

*Checkable text-vs-table items*

- **(i-a) Model 1 sidewalk, p. 8 vs. Table 3 (p. 9).** Text: "–.28 percentage points (s.e. = .11)". Table: "–.28** (.11)". **MATCH.**
- **(i-b) Model 1 streetlights.** Text: "–.19 (s.e. = .09)". Table: "–.19* (.09)". **MATCH.**
- **(i-c) Model 1 crosswalk.** Text: "(.002, s.e. = .16)", "not statistically significant". Table: ".002 (.16)", no stars. **MATCH.**
- **(i-d) Model 1 images / intersections.** Text: "coef. = .09, s.e. = .15; coef. = –.05, s.e. = .12". Table: ".09 (.15)"; "–.05 (.12)". **MATCH.**
- **(i-e) Model 1 verbal translation.** Text: "a little more than a quarter" (–.28) and "approximately one-fifth" (–.19). **MATCH.**
- **(i-f) Model 2 sidewalk.** Text: "–.25 points (s.e. = .11)". Table: "–.25* (.11)". **MATCH.**
- **(i-g) Model 2 streetlights.** Text: "–.39 (s.e. = .11)". Table: "–.39*** (.12)". **MISMATCH** (the SE).
- **(i-h) Model 2 other image indicators.** Text: non-single-family homes and signage "predict higher levels"; fencing, greenery, and single-lane roads "not significant". Table: .50*** (.15), .26* (.11); .25 (.13), .15 (.08), .12 (.08), no stars. **MATCH.**
- **(i-i) Model 2 crosswalk/images/intersections.** Text: "all remain below the threshold". Table: –.08 (.17), .13 (.16), –.17 (.12), no stars. **MATCH.**
- **(i-j) Model 2 "does not lead to a substantial change".** Streetlights move from –.19 to –.39, which roughly doubles. The text calls this an increase "somewhat." **AMBIGUOUS** (the wording understates the change).
- **(ii-a) Discussion streetlight SD, p. 10 vs. Table 2 (p. 8).** Text: "around 10 percentage points". Table 2 All: streetlights SD 9.74. **MATCH.**
- **(ii-b) Discussion streetlight effect vs. Table 3.** Text: "around 0.4 percentage point decrease ... on average". Model 2: –.39. Model 3: –.41, but that is the suburban slope, not an average. **MATCH** with Model 2, which the text does not name.
- **(ii-c) Discussion sidewalk SD vs. Table 2.** Text: "around 27 percentage points". Table 2 All: sidewalk SD 27.25. **MATCH.**
- **(ii-d) Discussion sidewalk effect vs. Table 3.** Text: "a .2 percentage point reduction". Table 3: –.28 (M1), –.25 (M2), –.48 (M3 suburban). **MISMATCH.** It understates, and it conflicts with p. 8's "a little more than a quarter."
- **(ii-e) Discussion heterogeneity restatement vs. Figure 2.** Text: sidewalks "highest in suburban"; streetlights "highest in rural". Figure 2 point estimates: sidewalks suburban –.48 is the most negative; streetlights rural ≈ –.63 is the most negative. **MATCH** on point estimates, with no significance qualifier.
- **(iii-a) Figure 2 reproduces Table 3 Model 3.** Sidewalks: urban –.48+.40 = –.08, suburban –.48, rural –.48+.48 = .00. Streetlights: urban –.41+.10 = –.31, suburban –.41, rural –.41–.22 = –.63. Crosswalks: urban –.23+.38 = .15, suburban –.23, rural –.23+.46 = .23. The figure reads ≈ –.08 / –.48 / –.01; –.30 / –.41 / –.63; .15 / –.24 / .22. The suburban bars (≈ –.75 to –.21; –.67 to –.14) equal ±1.96 × Table 3 SE, which implies 95% CIs. **MATCH.**
- **(iii-b) "Sidewalks only have a strong relationship ... in suburban areas" (p. 9).** Figure 2: suburban interval excludes 0; urban (≈ –.39 to .22) and rural (≈ –.58 to .56) include 0. Table 3: Sidewalk*urban .40* (.17) is significant; Sidewalk*rural .48 (.31) is not. **AMBIGUOUS.** The claim is true as "only suburban is distinguishable from zero." The rural–suburban difference is not significant, and the rural CI contains the suburban estimate.
- **(iii-c) Streetlights "twice as important in rural areas as urban ones" and "strong ... everywhere" (p. 9).** Point estimates: –.63 / –.31 = 2.0. Table 3: Streetlights*urban .10 (.15) and Streetlights*rural –.22 (.22), neither significant. Figure 2: the urban interval's upper bound is ≈ –.03, and the rural and urban intervals overlap heavily. **AMBIGUOUS.** The ratio matches the point estimates, but neither the difference nor "strong ... everywhere" is supported inferentially.
- **(iii-d) "Figure 2 displays the coefficients ... for sidewalks and streetlights" (p. 9) vs. Figure 2.** The figure has three panels, including crosswalks. **MISMATCH** (minor; the crosswalk panel goes undescribed).
- **(iii-e) Model 3 interactions discussed in prose.** Intersections*urban –.38* (.18) is significant in Table 3 and never mentioned; it bears on the p. 10 claim that intersection density does not predict. **AMBIGUOUS** (an omission, not a contradiction).
- **(iv) Data year: p. 1 intro vs. abstract vs. pp. 3–4.** Intro: "the 2019 NCES Common Core of Data and the Office of Civil Rights". Abstract: "2018–2019". p. 3: OCR "2018–19 school year". p. 4: CCD "2018–19". **AMBIGUOUS.** "2019" is probably shorthand, not a contradiction. *Reviewer's external note, not checkable in the paper:* to my knowledge, OCR's Civil Rights Data Collection was fielded for 2017–18 and then 2020–21, not 2018–19. National 2018–19 school-level chronic absenteeism is usually drawn from ED's EDFacts files. The paper does not name the specific file, so readers who need the exact source should verify it.
- **(v-a) Table 2: "more than five times the rate" (p. 7).** 27.47 / 5.33 = 5.15. **MATCH.**
- **(v-b) Table 2: "more likely to serve high school grades".** High: 11.18 → 19.48 → 35.31. **MATCH.**
- **(v-c) Table 2: "students with fewer socioeconomic resources".** FRL 37.76 → 62.48; advantage .36 → –.31; disadvantage –.17 → .27. **MATCH.**
- **(v-d) Table 2: "located in rural or urban areas".** Urban 40.39 → 52.65; rural 12.39 → 16.65; suburban 51.07 → 36.34. **MATCH** in direction, although the shares themselves are problematic (v-g).
- **(v-e) Table 2: census physical measures "do not vary dramatically".** Year built 1977 / 1976 / 1973 and car ownership 87.55 / 88.35 / 84.63 are roughly flat. Population density 298.11 → 345.71 → 561.55 is up 88%. **MISMATCH** for population density.
- **(v-f) Table 2: "fewer single-family homes, more commercial activity, and less greenery".** Not-single-family 24.25 → 31.34; signs 21.58 → 25.70; >30% green 86.75 → 83.81. **MATCH.**
- **(v-g) Table 2 urbanicity shares vs. p. 4 definitions.** p. 4 defines mutually exclusive categories. Table 2 sums: 103.85 / 105.72 / 105.64 / 105.08 (All). **MISMATCH** (an internal inconsistency).
- **(v-h) Table 2 population density units.** The label reads "(1000s per square mile)". The All mean of 403.39 would mean ≈ 403,000 per square mile, which is implausible. **MISMATCH** (unit label).
- **(v-i) Table 2 middle grades, lowest vs. highest third.** Both are "37.26 (48.35)". The All value 37.60 is consistent within rounding. **AMBIGUOUS** (possible duplication).
- **(v-j) Table 2 "Neighborhood average year built" vs. p. 4 "median year that buildings in the tract were built".** **MISMATCH** (minor label inconsistency).
- **(vi-a) Table 1: "strongest correlation ... non-single-family homes and greenery (.79)" (p. 7).** Table 1: "–.79". It is the largest in absolute value (next are .71 and .70). **MISMATCH** (sign omitted).
- **(vi-b) Table 1: sidewalks "highly correlated with ... signs and the number of images and intersections".** Table 1: .68, .70, .71. **MATCH.**
- **(vi-c) Table 1: "correlations are surprisingly low" and "not high enough ... to be concerned about multicollinearity".** Table 1 has several at .63–.79, including sidewalks–streetlights .67 (not mentioned). **AMBIGUOUS** (an interpretive tension; no VIFs are reported).
- **(vi-d) Table 1: NSF homes, greenery, and fencing "not highly correlated" with walkability measures.** Sidewalks/streetlights: NSF .44/.41; green –.31/–.43; fencing .17/.35. **MATCH.** Signs, which are not in that list, run .68/.68.
- **(vii-a) Sample: p. 3 "more than 78,000" vs. Table 2 N and Table 3 schools.** 78,416 in both. **MATCH.**
- **(vii-b) Tercile Ns vs. total.** 25,877 + 25,878 + 26,661 = 78,416. **MATCH.**
- **(vii-c) "Around 3% of schools with valid locations are excluded" (p. 3).** No base count, and no counts for the <25-student or alternative/special-education exclusions, are given anywhere. **AMBIGUOUS** (cannot be verified).
- **(vii-d) Number of districts.** Table 3: 14,147 in all models. It is never mentioned in the text, and the number of single-school districts (which contribute nothing to within-district estimates) is not reported. **AMBIGUOUS.**
- **(viii-a) Source lines.** Tables 1, 2, 3 and Figure 2 read "Author's calculations" on a three-author paper. **MISMATCH** (production).
- **(viii-b) Figure 2 caption vs. figure title.** Caption: "Predicted marginal effect of walkability infrastructure". In-figure title: "Average Marginal Effect by Metropolitan Location". The note says "Average marginal effects"; the p. 9 text says "coefficients (i.e., marginal effects)". **AMBIGUOUS** (inconsistent terminology, same object).
- **(viii-c) Figure 2 note, "when the predictor changes by one standard deviation", vs. the crosswalk panel.** Crosswalk is a binary indicator (p. 6), and Table 3's note standardizes only "continuous variables." **AMBIGUOUS.**
- **(viii-d) Table 3 note completeness.** There is no statement of the omitted metro category (suburban), district FE, or district-clustered SEs, which appear only on p. 7. **AMBIGUOUS** (self-containment gap).
- **(viii-e) Table 3 constant vs. Table 2 mean.** 15.97–16.18 vs. 15.09. These are not directly comparable because of the reference categories and FE normalization. **Not a discrepancy.**
- **(ix-a) H1 answered explicitly?** Yes, p. 8 ("support for both hypotheses") and p. 10 ¶1. **MATCH.**
- **(ix-b) H2 answered explicitly?** It is declared supported on p. 8 and restated on p. 10. H2 names crosswalks, which are null in Models 1–3, and no formal comparison of predictive strength is reported. **AMBIGUOUS** (overstated as full support).
- **(x-a) Typographical and production errors.** A missing period after "(Chalkley et al., 2018)" (p. 3). "car ownerships" (p. 7). A stray comma in "socioeconomic status, and urban development" (p. 10). The variable is labeled "Not-" in the Table 1 header, Table 2, and p. 8, but "Non-single-family" in the Table 1 row, Table 3, and p. 5. "Street Lights" in Figure 2 vs. "Streetlights" everywhere else. **MISMATCH** (production).
- **(x-b) Equation rendering (p. 7, eq. 2).** It is rendered cleanly, but β1 labels both W and W·I, so the interaction coefficient has no distinct symbol. **MISMATCH** (notation).
- **(x-c) Terminology, p. 8.** The text says heterogeneity tests address "nonlinearities", but the models are interactions (effect modification). **AMBIGUOUS** (mislabeling).
- **(x-d) Terminology, p. 7 vs. p. 4 / Table 2.** p. 7 has "car usage"; p. 4 and Table 2 have "own a car" / "percent car ownership". **AMBIGUOUS** (minor).
