### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper's real contribution is a new national, school-level linkage. It joins computer-vision measures of sidewalks, streetlights, and crosswalks within one mile of about 78,000 U.S. public schools to 2018–19 chronic absenteeism rates, and it documents a small, statistically detectable within-district association: about −0.25 to −0.48 percentage points per SD of sidewalk or streetlight prevalence, or 2–4% of the outcome's SD (Table 3, p. 9; Table 2, p. 8). That is a useful descriptive fact and a proof of concept for bringing scalable built-environment imagery into attendance research. The paper's most quotable claims go further than this evidence can take them: "small tweaks" (p. 2), "relatively cost-effective" (p. 10), "tip of the iceberg" (p. 10), and the busing-route recommendation (p. 10). Its second hypothesis, that direct measures beat proxies, is supported only by a non-significance pattern, not by a head-to-head test. So does its claim of rural and suburban heterogeneity (p. 9).

**Strengths:**

- **A new linkage at national scale.** Machine-learning street-imagery measures (164 million images, p. 4) are joined to near-universe school data: 78,416 schools in 14,147 districts (Table 3, p. 9). The imagery itself comes from prior public-health work (pp. 5–6). The new part is connecting it to an education outcome for the whole country.
- **A sensible comparison design for a descriptive paper.** District fixed effects absorb district policy, reporting practice, and region (pp. 6–7). The controls are rich: school demographics, tract advantage and disadvantage indices, and image-based controls for land use (Model 2). Standard errors are clustered by district (p. 7).
- **The main association survives adding correlated land-use image controls.** In Model 2, sidewalks go from −.28 to −.25 and streetlights from −.19 to −.39 (Table 3, p. 9). That gives some reassurance that the direct-infrastructure coefficients are not just stand-ins for commercial density. The paper also adds substantive framing that yellow-bus and transit studies have mostly left implicit: walkers face transportation barriers too (pp. 1–3).
- **Honest about the outcome being blunt, and about the unmeasured subjective side of walking** (p. 4, p. 10).

**Weaknesses:**

- **The magnitudes are small, and the policy language outruns them.** The preferred estimates are −.25 (sidewalks) and −.39 (streetlights) percentage points per SD (Table 3, Model 2, p. 9). Against an outcome SD of 11.87 and a mean of 15.09 (Table 2, p. 8), that is 2.1% and 3.3% of an SD. For a school of average size (584 students, Table 2), it works out to about 1.5–2.3 fewer chronically absent students. A 1-SD change is also not a "small tweak" (p. 2): it means 27 more percentage points of all imagery within a mile showing sidewalks (Table 2 SD 27.25; p. 10).
- **No cost data supports the cost-effectiveness claim.** The Discussion's cost comparison names crossing guards (p. 10), which are not measured. The paper's own crosswalk estimate is a null (Table 3: .002, −.08, −.23, all n.s.).
- **H2 ("direct measures will be better predictors than road network or intersection density," p. 3) is not tested as stated.** The evidence is that image and intersection counts are non-significant *conditional on* sidewalk measures they correlate with at .70–.71 (Table 1, p. 7). There is no head-to-head model and no fit comparison. In Model 2, the intersection estimate (−.17, s.e. .12) is statistically indistinguishable from the sidewalk estimate (−.25, s.e. .11). One of the three named direct measures, crosswalks, is null throughout. And in urban areas the proxy is significant (Intersections×urban −.38*, Table 3 continued, p. 9).
- **The heterogeneity claims (p. 9) outrun the interaction tests.** Two of ten Model 3 interactions reach p < .05. The streetlight pattern described as "twice as important in rural areas" rests on non-significant interactions (Streetlights×rural −.22, s.e. .22; ×urban .10, s.e. .15). The authors also tested interactions with "all school variables and census variables" (p. 8) and report only this one dimension, with no joint test.
- **The raw gradient runs the opposite way.** Before adjustment, the highest-absenteeism third of schools has *more* sidewalks and streetlights (Table 2, p. 8). The protective association appears only after conditioning on correlated covariates. The streetlight coefficient doubles when the image controls are added (Model 1 → 2). *Interpretive:* both facts signal that the estimate depends on specification, and that makes a causal reading especially risky.
- **The mechanism is not observed.** There are no data on travel mode, walk distance, or bus eligibility (p. 10). The one available proxy for car dependence shows no heterogeneity (car-ownership interactions, p. 8), which is the opposite of what the walking mechanism predicts.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite it for:** the fact that, within U.S. districts in 2018–19, schools surrounded by more image-detected sidewalks and streetlights had slightly lower chronic absenteeism after demographic, tract, and land-use adjustment. The size is about 0.25–0.4 percentage points per SD, or 2–3% of an SD (Table 3, Model 2).
- **Cite it for:** a feasibility demonstration that national computer-vision built-environment measures can be linked to school outcomes, and for the descriptive correlation structure of those measures around schools (Table 1).
- **Do not cite it for** causal effects of sidewalks or streetlights on attendance. It is a single cross-section with school-location (not student-route) exposure and no source of exogenous variation.
- **Do not cite it for** "small tweaks" producing "meaningful changes," or for cost-effectiveness. The estimates are for 1-SD shifts across a whole one-mile radius, and the paper collects no cost data.
- **Do not cite it for** the claim that direct image measures outperform density proxies (H2). That claim rests on the non-significance of highly collinear covariates, not on a comparative test, and crosswalks, a direct measure, are null.
- **Do not cite it for** "streetlights matter most in rural areas" or "sidewalks matter only in suburbs" as established findings. The streetlight interactions are non-significant, and the rural sidewalk estimate is uninformative (wide CI, Figure 2), not a demonstrated zero.
- **Do not cite it for** the busing-route recommendation. No route, walk-zone, or bus-eligibility data were analyzed (p. 10).
- **Open questions:** whether the association is causal, for example through changes over time in sidewalk or streetlight installation or through student-level route exposure; whether it holds after the pandemic, when chronic absenteeism roughly doubled (p. 1); and how accurate the classifiers are for rare features (precision and recall are not reported).

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Novelty.* **Interpretive:** the question is well motivated and only partly new. That transportation barriers affect attendance is established in the work the paper cites (Gottfried, 2017; Stein & Grigg, 2019; Burdick-Will & Stein, 2024; Edwards, 2023; pp. 1–2). The extension to *walking infrastructure* is a real, if incremental, conceptual addition. The imagery data are not new; the authors cite earlier health applications (Keralis et al., 2020; Q. C. Nguyen et al., 2019, 2022; Yue et al., 2022; p. 6). The novelty is the linkage and its scale. Earlier Street View work on schools used labor-intensive virtual audits (McCoy et al., 2022, cited p. 3). Within the paper's own framing, this looks like the first national estimate of its kind. I have not independently surveyed the literature for competing national studies.

*Significance at credible strength.* **Interpretive:** read correctly, as a conditional cross-sectional association, the finding is modest but not trivial. Chronic absenteeism is a first-order policy problem. A measurable, direction-consistent correlation with ordinary infrastructure is worth knowing, and the fixed effects plus land-use image controls make it more than a density artifact. But the Discussion recasts the association as something a district could act on, and that move is where the contribution is oversold.

- *"Even small tweaks … could lead to meaningful changes" (p. 2).* The unit of change behind every estimate is 1 SD of the *share of all street imagery within a mile* containing the feature: about 27 points for sidewalks and 10 points for streetlights (p. 10; Table 2). **Interpretive, approximate:** images are sampled every 100 m with four views per point (p. 4), and the mean school has about 3,000 images (Table 2). That implies on the order of 75 km of sampled road per radius. A 27-point sidewalk shift would then mean new sidewalks along roughly 20 km of road. That is not a tweak, and even that change is associated with about 1.5 fewer chronically absent students in an average-size school.
- *"Relatively cost-effective" and the crossing-guard comparison (p. 10).* No cost or feasibility data are analyzed. The Discussion also compares these per-SD associations with effect sizes from randomized or quasi-experimental attendance interventions (Eklund et al., 2022; p. 10). That is not a like-for-like comparison: one side is a causal effect of an intervention, the other a cross-sectional gradient.
- *"Tip of the iceberg" (p. 10).* The argument is that a blunt outcome understates the true relationship. That is plausible for measurement dilution, but it is one-sided. Unmeasured within-district confounding could bias the estimate in either direction. Crossing municipal boundaries within a county district, for example, can change both infrastructure and other public services. The raw gradient is also in the *opposite* direction (Table 2). The paper has no basis for signing the net bias.
- *Busing routes (p. 10).* **Interpretive:** "think carefully about where students would feel comfortable walking" is reasonable advice. But it does not follow from these analyses, which use a straight-line radius around the school's coordinates (p. 6) and cannot tell bus-eligible from walk-zone students (p. 10).

*H2 and the "direct beats proxy" methodological claim.* The paper concludes that "this study demonstrates the benefits of direct, image-based measures" (p. 10). The evidence is that images and intersections are non-significant in Models 1–2 while sidewalks and streetlights are significant (Table 3, p. 9; text p. 8). **Interpretive:** that does not test H2. When covariates correlate at .70–.71 (Table 1), how significance splits among them is not a measure of comparative predictive power. The paper reports no model with proxies alone, no incremental R², and no test of equal coefficients. Within-R² is .30 in all three models (Table 3), so readers cannot tell how much the walkability block adds at all. The paper's own results also cut against H2 twice. Crosswalks, one of the three direct measures named in H2 (p. 3), are null in every model. And the urban intersection interaction is significant (−.38*, Table 3 continued), which implies an urban intersection slope of about −.31, as large as the urban streetlight slope. At most, H2 is "not contradicted for sidewalks and streetlights."

*Heterogeneity by metropolitan location.* The Model 3 main effects are the suburban slopes, as the interaction structure and Figure 2 imply. From the table, the implied slopes are: sidewalks −.08 urban, −.48 suburban, 0.00 rural; streetlights −.31 urban, −.41 suburban, −.63 rural (Table 3, p. 9; consistent with Figure 2, p. 6).

- **Checkable:** the sidewalk urban–suburban difference is significant (.40*, s.e. .17). The rural–suburban difference is not (.48, s.e. .31), and the rural sidewalk CI in Figure 2 runs from roughly −.6 to +.6. "Sidewalks only have a strong relationship … in suburban areas" (p. 9) is defensible for urban versus suburban. For rural areas it reflects imprecision, not a demonstrated absence.
- **Checkable:** neither streetlight interaction is significant (×urban .10, s.e. .15; ×rural −.22, s.e. .22). "Streetlights have a strong relationship … everywhere but are twice as important in rural areas" (p. 9) describes point estimates only. The urban interval in Figure 2 nearly reaches zero, and an urban slope of −.31 is 2.6% of an outcome SD, which is hard to call "strong."
- **Interpretive:** the paper tested interactions with every school and census variable (p. 8), found "no evidence of meaningful heterogeneity" there (results not shown), and reports one dimension in which 2 of 10 terms cross p < .05, with no joint test. Readers should treat the heterogeneity story as exploratory. That includes the explanations offered for it: ambient light in rural areas, and sidewalk condition versus existence in cities.

*Measurement.* Classifier accuracy is reported as overall agreement: sidewalks 84.5%, streetlights 88%, crosswalks 97.2% (pp. 5–6). **Interpretive:** for rare classes, overall accuracy says little without base rates, precision, and recall. Streetlights appear in about 14.5% of images near schools (Table 2). In that setting, a classifier that always says "absent" would reach about 85% accuracy, so 88% is not reassuring on its face. The test-set class balance is not reported here (the paper points to Yue et al., 2022), so this is a question, not a finding. Misclassification that correlates with neighborhood type, such as image quality or tree cover, could bias the comparisons *between* features that H2 relies on. The imagery was collected in November 2019, just after the outcome year (p. 4). The authors' justification is reasonable and I do not consider this a major threat.

*Generalizability.* **Checkable:** the sample covers essentially all regular U.S. public schools with at least 25 students and complete data; about 3% of schools with valid locations are dropped (p. 3). **Interpretive:** that breadth is a real strength for external validity *within the pre-pandemic U.S. in 2018–19*. Three boundaries deserve more emphasis than the paper gives them:

1. Chronic absenteeism has roughly doubled since then (13% → 28%, p. 1), and its drivers may have shifted.
2. Identification is within district, and districts with a single school contribute nothing. Many rural districts are small, so the rural estimates rest on comparatively few within-district contrasts, which fits their wide intervals.
3. Exposure is measured around the school's coordinates, not along students' routes. That matters most for charter and magnet schools, which draw from wide areas (p. 4).

*Standing in the literature.* **Interpretive:** this is now the broadest descriptive evidence on the specific link between walkability infrastructure and chronic absenteeism. It is not the best evidence that transportation affects attendance generally; the causal work it cites (for example, on bus provision and transit) remains stronger on that. It sets up clear follow-on work: difference-in-differences or event-study designs using dated sidewalk and streetlight installations (for example, Safe Routes to School grants) or time-varying imagery; student-level models with residential addresses and routes and walk-zone discontinuities; post-pandemic replication; and fuller classifier validation. Public release of the school-level measures would make it much more useful.

**Checkable items** (facts relied on; everything else above labeled interpretive):

- Sample: 78,416 schools, 14,147 districts (Table 3, p. 9; Table 2 N, p. 8); about 3% of located schools excluded for missing data; schools under 25 students excluded (p. 3).
- Outcome: mean 15.09, SD 11.87; tercile means 5.33 / 12.12 / 27.47 (Table 2, p. 8).
- Raw gradient: sidewalks 42.02 (lowest third) vs. 44.45 (highest third); streetlights 13.55 vs. 15.56 (Table 2, p. 8).
- Exposure SDs: sidewalks 27.25, streetlights 9.74; mean images 3.00 thousand; mean enrollment 584 (Table 2, p. 8). Images every 100 m, four views per point, 164 million total, collected November 2019 (p. 4).
- Model 1: sidewalk −.28** (.11); streetlights −.19* (.09); crosswalk .002 (.16); images .09 (.15); intersections −.05 (.12) (Table 3, p. 9).
- Model 2: sidewalk −.25* (.11); streetlights −.39*** (.12); crosswalk −.08 (.17); images .13 (.16); intersections −.17 (.12); non-single-family homes .50***; signs .26* (Table 3, p. 9).
- Model 3 main effects (suburban reference): sidewalk −.48*** (.14); streetlights −.41** (.14); crosswalk −.23 (.22); intersections .07 (.14). Interactions: sidewalk×urban .40* (.17), ×rural .48 (.31); streetlights×urban .10 (.15), ×rural −.22 (.22); crosswalk×urban .38 (.41), ×rural .46 (.39); images×urban .31 (.22), ×rural −1.20 (.70); intersections×urban −.38* (.18), ×rural .29 (.30) (Table 3 continued, p. 9).
- Within-R² .30, between .14, overall .24 in all three models (Table 3, p. 9).
- Figure 2 (p. 6): suburban sidewalk slope about −.48 with CI excluding 0; urban and rural sidewalk CIs include 0 (rural roughly −.6 to +.6); streetlight rural point about −.63; urban streetlight CI upper bound near 0; all crosswalk CIs include 0.
- Correlations: sidewalks with images .70, with intersections .71, with signs .68; streetlights with signs .68 (Table 1, p. 7).
- Classifier accuracy: sidewalks 84.5%, streetlights 88%, crosswalks 97.2% (pp. 5–6); no precision or recall reported.
- Heterogeneity tested against all school and census variables, with only metro location reported as meaningful; car-ownership interaction null (p. 8).
- H1 and H2 wording (p. 3). "Small tweaks … meaningful changes" (p. 2). "Relatively cost-effective" and "tip of the iceberg" (p. 10). "About 0.4" and ".2" per-SD summaries (p. 10; the sidewalk figure rounds Model 2's −.25 down). The busing-route recommendation (Conclusion, p. 10). The admission that bus-eligible students cannot be distinguished (p. 10).
- Effect-size conversions (arithmetic on the above): .25/11.87 = 2.1% SD; .39/11.87 = 3.3% SD; .48/11.87 = 4.0% SD; .63/11.87 = 5.3% SD. At 584 students, .25–.39 pp ≈ 1.5–2.3 students.
- No online appendix or supplementary material was available for this review. Unshown results (the non-metro interaction tests; the logged-outcome robustness check in footnote 1, p. 11) could not be checked.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper states the headline model clearly: a school-level linear model with district fixed effects and district-clustered robust SEs (p. 7, Eq. 1), with N, district counts, and R-squared reported (p. 9, Table 3). Most of the covariates come from public federal files. But the variables the paper is about, the Street View sidewalk, streetlight, and crosswalk shares within 1 mile of each school, come from an unshared computer-vision dataset of 164 million images. That dataset cannot be regenerated from what the paper reports (pp. 4–6). The PDF has no data-availability statement, no code or replication-package statement, no software statement, and no supplementary materials (p. 11 back matter). Several reported results (the full heterogeneity battery, p. 8, and the logged-outcome check, p. 11 fn. 1) are asserted without any numbers. As published, the central coefficients cannot be independently checked. A reader can verify Table 3's internal arithmetic but has to take the key measures on trust.

**Strengths:**

- Headline specification is stated unambiguously at the level of model form: outcome = percent chronically absent; district fixed effects; school-level error; "All standard errors are robust and clustered at the district level" (p. 7, Eq. 1–2). Covariate blocks W, S, N, G are enumerated in words (p. 7).
- Table 3 (p. 9) reports every coefficient with SEs for all three models, plus within/between/overall R-squared (.30/.14/.24), N = 78,416 schools and 14,147 districts in every column, so the estimation sample is constant across models.
- Table 2 (p. 8) gives means and SDs for every analytic variable by outcome tercile and overall (N = 25,877 / 25,878 / 26,661 / 78,416), and Table 1 (p. 7) gives the image-measure correlation matrix. Together they allow useful consistency checks. For example, the tercile-weighted outcome mean reproduces the overall mean of 15.09, and the binary-variable SDs match sqrt(p(1-p)).
- Figure 2 (p. 6) point estimates can be reconstructed exactly from Table 3 Model 3 main effects plus interactions (e.g., streetlights: suburban −.41, urban −.41+.10 = −.31, rural −.41−.22 = −.63), with suburban as the implied reference category.
- The Street View acquisition protocol is described concretely: Google Street View API, 640×640 px, one sample point every 100 m of road, 4 headings (0/90/180/270°), 164 million images, captured November 2019 (p. 4). Per-indicator classification accuracies are reported (p. 5–6: sidewalks 84.5%, streetlights 88%, crosswalks 97.2%, etc.).
- The outcome and covariate sources are named public federal collections (OCR/ED chronic absenteeism, NCES CCD 2018–19, ACS 2015–2019 5-year; pp. 3–4). The advantage and disadvantage index components are listed item by item (p. 4).

**Weaknesses:**

- **No data-availability, code, or materials statement anywhere in the PDF** (checked the full text and the p. 11 back matter: Acknowledgments, ORCID, Funding, Conflicts, Note 1). The PDF contains no hyperlinks other than the Crossmark badge (p. 1), and no supplementary material or online appendix is referenced. For a 2026 journal article, this falls below current norms.
- **The key independent variables depend on an unshared, non-regenerable derived dataset.** The CNN pipeline section (pp. 4–5) gives the train/validation/test split (80/20) and says "each model architecture was trained multiple times". It does not name the architecture or report the number of labeled images, the labeling protocol, hyperparameters, random seeds, the mean/SD of error across runs, or precision/recall. For crosswalks (a rare, intersection-only feature, p. 6), accuracy alone says little. The paper defers to Yue et al. (2022) "for more details" (p. 5). The "separate, semi-supervised learning approach" is described only as "consistent" with the reported accuracies, with no numbers (p. 6). Image capture dates are not reported, although the argument that most imagery predates 2018–19 (p. 4) depends on them.
- **Heterogeneity analysis is largely unreported.** Pp. 7–8 say interactions with every school and census variable were tested ("We do not find evidence of meaningful heterogeneity", p. 8, including car ownership). Only the metro-location interactions are tabulated (Table 3 Model 3, p. 9; Figure 2, p. 6). No coefficients, p-values, or joint tests are given for the others. The claim that "results are essentially identical" when walkability measures are interacted one at a time (p. 7) is also unreported.
- **The logged-outcome robustness check (p. 11, fn. 1) reports no estimates.** It also does not say how the 95 zero-absenteeism schools were "imputed" (constant added? value substituted?).
- **Sample construction cannot be reproduced to the stated N.** P. 3 gives criteria but no count flow: "regular public schools (as defined by the National Center for Education Statistics)", exclusion of alternative/special-education-only schools, ≥25 students, and "Around 3%" dropped for missing chronic absenteeism or demographics. There is no starting N, no N at each step, no handling of schools with no Street View coverage within 1 mile, and no handling of tract-match failures.
- **Outcome vintage and source are ambiguous (flag, not adjudicated from the PDF alone).** The paper attributes 2018–19 school-level chronic absenteeism to the "Office of Civil Rights" (p. 3; abstract p. 1). The CRDC is a biennial collection. See Detailed Commentary for what I could and could not verify online.
- **Internal inconsistency in Table 2 (p. 8):** urban, suburban, and rural shares sum to more than 100% in every column (All: 45.27 + 44.82 + 14.99 = 105.08; lowest third 103.85; middle 105.72; highest 105.64). This happens even though the p. 4 definitions describe mutually exclusive categories. The binary SDs are each internally consistent with their means, so this is not a transcription of SDs. A replicator cannot tell which classification was actually used in Model 3.
- **No software, packages, or versions are reported** for either the regression analysis or the CNN pipeline.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the sidewalk and streetlight coefficients (Table 3, p. 9) as **unverifiable as published**. Anyone outside the author team cannot rebuild the school-level image shares. Before relying on the magnitudes, request from the authors (a) the school-level (NCES ID) derived walkability file and (b) the estimation code.
- Resolve the outcome source before attempting replication. Ask the authors which file they used: an ED/EDFacts 2018–19 chronic absenteeism release, or the CRDC (and which year). The outcome mean of 15.09% (Table 2) is one check you can run against whatever file you obtain.
- The regression mechanics can be partially checked without the image data. Table 2's overall SDs match the Discussion's "around 27" and "around 10" percentage-point SDs (p. 10). Figure 2 points follow from Table 3 Model 3 arithmetic. The within/between/overall R-squared format (Table 3) is the standard output of a one-way fixed-effects panel estimator. A replicator using a different FE routine should expect singleton-district handling to change N and R-squared.
- Discount the negative heterogeneity claims (p. 8) and the logged-outcome robustness (fn. 1, p. 11) to "author assertion". No numbers are available to check them. Of the heterogeneity battery, only the metro-location result is actually reported, so treat it as one reported test out of several run. The paper does not say how many.
- Ask the authors to reconcile the Table 2 urban/suburban/rural shares (sum ≈ 105%) and to name the metropolitan and central-city delineation vintage. Model 3's interaction estimates depend directly on this coding.
- Useful quick checks against public files: the charter (6.31%) and magnet (3.92%) shares, the elementary/middle/high grade-span shares, and the FRL/Black/Hispanic means (Table 2) can all be compared with CCD 2018–19 after applying the p. 3 restrictions. That at least tests whether the sample construction is roughly recoverable.
- Be aware that the Discussion's summary (sidewalks ".2 percentage point", p. 10) does not match either Model 1 (−.28) or Model 2 (−.25) in Table 3. The streetlight "around 0.4" matches Model 2 (−.39). Read the magnitudes from Table 3, not the prose.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What the paper makes transparent.* The regression layer is the best-documented part. Equation (1) and the p. 7 text define the outcome, the four covariate blocks, district fixed effects, and district-level clustered robust SEs. Table 3 (p. 9) reports all coefficients and SEs for three nested models, a constant, R-squared on three bases, and school and district counts. Figure 2 (p. 6) can be reconstructed from Table 3 Model 3: sidewalks urban −.48+.40 = −.08, suburban −.48, rural −.48+.48 = 0.00; crosswalks urban −.23+.38 = .15, rural −.23+.46 = .23. These match the plotted points. The figure's confidence intervals cannot be checked because they need interaction covariances that are not reported, and the CI level (presumably 95%) is not stated in the caption. The caption and text (p. 9) describe the figure as showing sidewalks and streetlights, but it also plots crosswalks. This is cosmetic. Table 2 is internally coherent in several ways I checked. The tercile-weighted mean of chronic absenteeism, (25,877×5.33 + 25,878×12.12 + 26,661×27.47)/78,416 ≈ 15.10, matches the reported 15.09. Binary-variable SDs match their means (e.g., Any crosswalk 92.12 → SD 26.94; Urban 45.27 → SD 49.78).

*What is taken on trust.* The analysis depends on the image-derived measures, and a reader cannot reach them. Reproducing them would require re-querying the Street View API for the same November 2019 panoramas at 100 m spacing across all US roads. It would also require the trained classifiers, and the paper provides neither weights, architecture, nor the labeled training set. My interpretive judgment is that a reader should treat these indicators as effectively non-regenerable by an outside team. Current API imagery differs from the 2019 capture, and the paper provides no model artifacts. A replicator therefore depends entirely on the authors releasing the derived school-level (or point-level) indicator file. What I verified online is separate from what the paper states. A targeted search found an openICPSR deposit (project 115264) from earlier Nguyen-lab work (Keralis et al., 2020) with tract-level aggregates built from about 31 million images. Search-result text from Yue et al. (2022) also indicates that neighborhood-level Street View data are available through a geoportal. Neither appears to be the 164-million-image, point-level data needed to build 1-mile school buffers, and this paper cites neither as a data source. I found no replication package for this article in a targeted search. That absence is from a quick search, not a definitive check.

The choice of image-indicator controls (block G) matters for the headline coefficients. The streetlight coefficient roughly doubles from Model 1 to Model 2 (−.19 to −.39, Table 3, p. 9) when G is added. So the unshared "nuisance" indicators (non-single-family homes, signs, fences, greenness, single-lane roads), whose accuracies are 82–95% (pp. 5–6), shape the result the paper emphasizes in the Discussion (p. 10). This is an interpretive point about why verification matters here, not a critique of identification.

*OCR/CRDC vintage.* The paper says school-level chronic absenteeism "come[s] from the Office of Civil Rights during the 2018–19 school year" (p. 3). The CRDC is biennial. Targeted online checks (Attendance Works and Brookings summaries of CRDC/EDFacts) indicate that the CRDC collected school-level chronic absence for 2013–14 and 2015–16. From 2017–18 onward, collection moved to ED's EDFacts system, and the next CRDC chronic-absence release covered 2020–21 because of the pandemic delay. If that is correct, no 2018–19 CRDC file exists, and the data are more likely an EDFacts release (or the CRDC 2017–18 file mislabeled). I could not confirm this from the PDF. The discrepancy is something a replicator must resolve with the authors, not something I can adjudicate. A one-year difference would also change the timing argument on p. 4 about the November 2019 imagery.

*Checkable items* (what the PDF does and does not state):

- Data-availability statement: **absent** (full text; p. 11 back matter contains Acknowledgments, ORCID, Funding [JHU Discovery Award], Conflicts, Note 1 only).
- Code / replication package / "available upon request": **absent** (entire PDF).
- Supplementary materials or online appendix referenced: **absent** (entire PDF). The only hyperlink in the PDF is Crossmark (p. 1).
- Software and version (regression or CNN): **absent**.
- Random seeds / training-run statistics for CNN: **absent**. "Multiple training runs" are mentioned but their mean/SD are not reported (p. 5).
- CNN architecture, labeled-set size, labeling protocol: **absent** (deferred to Yue et al., 2022; p. 5).
- Train/val/test split: **present** (80% train+validation / 20% test; the train-vs-validation split within the 80% is not given; p. 4).
- Per-indicator classification accuracy: **present** (pp. 5–6). Precision/recall/prevalence: **absent**.
- Image acquisition parameters: **present** (640×640, 100 m spacing, 4 headings, 164M images, Nov 2019; p. 4). Image capture dates: **absent**.
- Outcome source and year: **present but ambiguous** (OCR, 2018–19, p. 3; see CRDC vintage note above).
- CCD year: **present** (2018–19, p. 4; "2019 NCES Common Core" on p. 1).
- ACS vintage: **present** (2015–2019 5-year, p. 4). Tract-boundary vintage and school-to-tract geocoding method: **absent**.
- Sample restrictions: **present as criteria** (regular schools per NCES; no alternative/special-ed-only; ≥25 students; ~3% dropped for missing data; p. 3). **Absent** as counts: no starting N, no step-wise Ns, no count for missing Street View coverage.
- Final N and districts: **present** (78,416 schools; 14,147 districts; Table 3, p. 9; tercile Ns, Table 2, p. 8). Tercile cut-points and tie handling: **absent** (unequal tercile Ns suggest ties).
- "Regular public school" definition: **ambiguous**. It references NCES but does not name the CCD school-type variable (p. 3).
- Charter/magnet flags: **present as concepts** (CCD indicators, p. 4). The CCD fields and handling of missing magnet flags are **absent**.
- Grade-span indicators: **present** (non-exclusive elementary <6th, middle 6–8, high >8th; p. 4).
- Urban/suburban/rural: **ambiguous**. "Central cities of any metropolitan area" (p. 4), with no delineation vintage (OMB CBSA year; "principal city" vs older "central city" concept) or data source. Table 2 shares sum to ~105% (p. 8), which conflicts with the mutually exclusive definition.
- Advantage/disadvantage indices: **present as components** (p. 4). Construction is **ambiguous**: "standardized sum of its elements" does not say whether elements are standardized before summing, or whether standardization is over tracts nationally or over schools. Table 2 reports overall SDs of 0.77 and 0.66 (p. 8), not 1.0, so the standardization base is not the analytic sample.
- Building age: **ambiguous**. "Median year that buildings in the tract were built" (p. 4) vs "average year built" (Tables 2–3).
- Population density units: **ambiguous**. Table 2 reports a mean of 403.39 "(1000s per square mile)" (p. 8), i.e., ~403,000 persons/sq mi, which is implausible for US tracts. The label is likely wrong.
- 1-mile straight-line radius from NCES lat/long: **present** (p. 6). Projection/geodesic method: **absent**.
- Image-share measures (percent of all images in radius) and crosswalk binary (any image in radius): **present** (p. 6). Whether shares are image-level or point-level is stated as "images".
- Intersection count: **present as a variable**, but the **data source is absent** (p. 6). The text does not say whether it comes from the Street View sampling network, TIGER, or OpenStreetMap.
- Standardization: **partially present**. "All continuous variables have been standardized" (Table 3 note, p. 9; p. 8). The outcome is evidently not standardized (coefficients in percentage points). The sample and level (overall vs within-district SD) are not stated. The Discussion's "around 27" and "around 10" point SDs (p. 10) match Table 2 overall SDs, suggesting standardization over the full analytic sample (my inference).
- Weighting: **absent** (no statement; unweighted school-level estimation presumably).
- Clustering: **present** (district-level, robust; p. 7).
- R-squared, N rows: **present** (Table 3, p. 9). They are sufficient to confirm constant sample across models, but not to verify coefficients without data.
- Footnote 1 logged outcome: **present as assertion, no numbers**; imputation method for 95 zeros **absent** (p. 11).
- Heterogeneity tests beyond metro location: **described but not reported** (pp. 7–8). Only Model 3 metro interactions are tabulated (Table 3, p. 9) and plotted (Figure 2, p. 6). Confirmed: no table or figure in the PDF reports interactions with grades, FRL, race, charter/magnet, size, tract indices, density, building age, or car ownership.
- Formal test of Hypothesis 2 ("better predictors", p. 3): **absent**. The support is inferred from significance patterns in Table 3 (p. 8).

*Steps a replicator would have to guess* (my judgment, not facts stated in the paper):

- Which chronic-absenteeism file and year to use (CRDC 2017–18 vs an EDFacts 2018–19 release), and how suppressed or masked values were treated.
- How "regular public school" and the ≥25-student threshold were operationalized in CCD (which enrollment field, which school-type code), and in what order the exclusions were applied, to arrive at 78,416.
- How schools were assigned to "districts" for the fixed effects. For example, are charter schools that are their own LEA treated as singleton districts, which would contribute nothing within-district and would affect the charter coefficient? Were singletons retained (the R-squared format suggests they may have been)?
- The metropolitan and central-city delineation used, and why Table 2 category shares exceed 100%.
- Whether the tract indices are sums of z-scores, means of z-scores, or re-standardized sums, and on what population they were standardized.
- The source and definition of the intersection count, and how the image count handles areas with no Street View coverage.
- The standardization base for all continuous regressors (full sample, overall SD, presumably).
- The imputation used for the 95 zero-outcome schools in the log specification.
- Everything about the CNN classifiers, and access to the point-level indicator file. A replicator is entirely dependent on the authors' derived dataset for W and G. There is no public route in the paper to rebuild them.
- Software and estimation routine. The within/between/overall R-squared suggests a standard one-way fixed-effects panel command, but this is not stated.

*Overall calibration.* Restricted or proprietary inputs are a legitimate constraint. Google's terms limit redistribution of raw imagery, and reasonable readers would not expect the 164 million images to be posted. But the derived school-level shares and the regression code are shareable in principle. The paper provides no statement about either, and no documented reason for their absence. The regression layer would be close to "adequate" on its own. The combination of (i) unshared core measures, (ii) unreported robustness and heterogeneity results, (iii) an ambiguous outcome vintage, and (iv) an unresolved Table 2 classification inconsistency means the central findings cannot currently be verified. That supports a "weak" rating. My confidence is moderate rather than high for two reasons. Yue et al. (2022) and related Nguyen-lab publications may document the pipeline more fully than I could check. And the authors may share derived data on request, which the paper neither promises nor rules out.
